cves.summary:
`SoftReadWriteLock` (and `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock`, which wraps one) checks once per lock object, by name, that `<path>.rw`, `<path>.rw/gen` and `<path>.rw/holders` are real directories and not symbolic links (files that redirect to another path). It then keeps only a boolean. Every later record operation resolves the full path again, and `O_NOFOLLOW` (a flag that makes an open fail when the final name is a symbolic link) protects the last component only. Another local user (the other user below) who can write the directory holding the lock, or who created `<path>.rw` first in a sticky directory such as `/tmp` (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), can put a tree under that name whose `gen` or `holders` is a symbolic link into a directory of the user running the lock (the lock user below).

A long-running process of the lock user that has already passed the check then creates, renames over and deletes files there with the lock user's privileges, including in `0700` directories the other user cannot open. The names and bytes are filelock's own lock records, not chosen by the other user. The scanner's reproducer replaces `.git/HEAD` in the lock user's private repository so that `git status` fails. There is no race. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.1.0 and <= 4.2.0. Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported it in private as `ANT-2026-WXXRI4M4` [high, CWE-367], titled "SoftReadWriteLock follows gen dir swapped for a symlink after first acquire".

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N, 3.3 (Low).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the swap happens between two acquisitions, with no race to win. `PR:L` (low privileges): a local user with ordinary privileges is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `I:L` (low integrity impact): the lock user's process replaces a file named `HEAD`, creates `epoch` and generation records, and deletes files whose names match the protocol's patterns, in any directory the lock user can write, with the lock user's privileges. The other user does not choose the bytes, but the files are gone and the chosen directory (a git repository) stops working. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock itself keeps working and the lock user's process does not stall. The scanner rated it high; we scored the vector for a lock user with ordinary privileges.

Classification from the external review: conditional security. It is a cross-user replacement of a cached `.rw` tree that redirects later writes of the lock user through an intermediate symbolic link. It needs a planted tree in sticky `/tmp` or a writable parent without the sticky bit. Scoring note: we rate integrity low rather than high. The bytes written through the swapped tree are filelock's own records, not content the other user chose, so the lower reading of the CVSS integrity metric applies.

## Scope and preconditions

- Trust boundary: the other party is a different local account with write access to the lock's parent directory. Without the sticky bit (a `0777` scratch or spool directory, or a group-writable project or cache directory shared with that account's group) write access alone is enough. The other user renames the lock user's own `0700` `<path>.rw` aside and puts its tree in place. In a sticky parent such as `/tmp` the extra precondition is that it created `<path>.rw` (with real `gen` and `holders` directories, mode `0777`) before the lock user's first acquire. `prepare()` accepts an existing tree whoever owns it, and the other user later replaces its own `gen` with a symbolic link. `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (a Linux setting that refuses to follow another user's symbolic link in a world-writable sticky directory) does not intervene, because the link sits inside the other user's own non-sticky `<path>.rw`, not in the sticky parent (the scanner ran with that setting).
- Lock user: any process that keeps one `SoftReadWriteLock` or `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock` object (a singleton per path by default) and acquires it more than once, or is waiting for it when the swap happens. A fresh process that meets the planted tree gets `RuntimeError`. Between two acquisitions there is no timing to win.
- Targets: any directory the lock user can write, on any filesystem. The other user needs only to know its path (`/home/victim/project/.git` in the reproducer, under a `0700` home directory the other user cannot open).
- Platform: observed on Linux. The code path is the same on every POSIX platform and on Windows, where a junction (a Windows directory that points at another directory) at a directory component plays the symbolic link's part. The scanner ran Linux only.
- Ancestor boundary: protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`, [`OsFiles.prepare` checks the three directories with `lstat` and caches `_prepared`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L121-L133). `lstat` reports what a name is without following a symbolic link. Every later operation takes a full path string, for example [`create`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L53-L60) (`O_NOFOLLOW` on the last component only), [`replace`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L86-L92) (`Path(source).replace(target)`), [`unlink`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L104-L112) and [`listdir`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L114-L119). The callers that write through the swapped tree are [`Participant.publish` / `_create_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L435-L445), [`GenerationLog._incarnation`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L282-L295) (creates `epoch`), [`commit`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L344-L360) (links a generation record and renames over `HEAD`), [`_keep_claim_fresh`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L487-L496), [`_sweep`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L498) and [`_list`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_protocol.py#L297) (unlink). There is one `OsFiles` per lock object ([`_sync.py` line 204](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L204)), handed to every `Participant` at [line 501](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L501).

## Introduced

The once-per-object shortcut (`_prepared`) came with `367b111` ("fix(soft-rw): publish the head through gen/HEAD (#799)", 2026-10-08), first released in 4.1.0 (verified with `git tag --contains 367b111`, which answers 4.1.0). That commit opens the route between two acquisitions with no timing to win. The check-then-use gap itself is older. At its parent `61582c5` (also first in 4.1.0) a contender already waiting during the swap still creates `epoch` in the target before the lock refuses it, while 4.0.0 leaves the target untouched in the same test. The group advisory carried `>= 4.0.0` as the union with a sibling finding; for this finding alone the range is `>= 4.1.0, <= 4.2.0`.

## Mechanism

`prepare()` runs `mkdir(mode=0o700)` and then `lstat()` on each of `<path>.rw`, `gen` and `holders`. It raises `RuntimeError("... exists but is not a directory or is a symlink; refusing to use it")` for a symbolic link or non-directory. It does this by name, once per `OsFiles` (`if self._prepared and not force: return`), and only a `FileNotFoundError` while creating the holder record (the file that says this process holds or wants the lock) leads to `prepare(force=True)`. All other `OsFiles` methods (`read`, `create`, `link`, `replace`, `overwrite`, `unlink`, `listdir`) take a full path string such as `/srv/shared/app.lock.rw/gen/HEAD`. `O_NOFOLLOW` applies to `HEAD`, and the kernel follows `app.lock.rw` and `gen` to whatever they name at that moment. The gap between the check and a use is therefore as long as the process keeps the lock object.

The scanner observed this at the scanned commit on Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14.8, overlayfs, with a default-options `SoftReadWriteLock`, as two accounts in `/srv/shared` (root-owned, mode `0777`, no sticky bit):

1. `victim` runs a worker that builds `SoftReadWriteLock("/srv/shared/app.lock")` once and takes `write_lock()` for each job. After the first job, `app.lock.rw` exists, owned by `victim`, mode `0700`.
2. `attacker` renames `app.lock.rw` to `app.lock.rw.aside`, creates a new `app.lock.rw` with a world-writable `holders/` in it, and makes `app.lock.rw/gen` a symbolic link to `/home/victim/project/.git`. `/home/victim/project` is mode `0700`; the `attacker` account cannot open anything below it.
3. The worker takes the lock for its second job. `write_lock()` returns without error. `/home/victim/project/.git` now holds new files `epoch`, `00000000000000000001` and `00000000000000000002`, and `<epoch>\nfilelock-rw/1\ngeneration=2\n` has replaced the content of `.git/HEAD`. `git status` there answers `fatal: not a git repository`.

The second acquisition, step by step: `Participant.publish()` calls `prepare()`, which returns at once, then creates `holders/<token>`. The planted tree has a writable `holders`, so this succeeds. `advance()` calls `GenerationLog.latest()` (the generation log is the lock's ordered record of write generations under `gen/`). `_incarnation()` reads `gen/epoch`, finds none behind the link, and creates `.git/epoch`. The epoch differs from the remembered one, so the code drops the remembered log. git's `HEAD` does not start with the new epoch, so `_head_record()` ignores it and the log reads as empty. `commit()` creates `.git/.commit-<token>`, hard-links it (a hard link is a second name for the same file) to `.git/00000000000000000001`, removes the temporary name, and publishes `HEAD` through `OsFiles.replace`, which is `rename(".git/.commit-<token>", ".git/HEAD")`. The release commits generation 2 the same way and renames over `HEAD` again.

Other ways into the same gap exist. The scanner ran each at this commit with a directory only the lock user can access as the link target. A contender already waiting when the swap happens recreates its missing holder record in the planted `holders/` on its next poll (`_keep_claim_fresh()`), and the commit that follows replaces `HEAD` in the target. A process that only holds and releases, with the tree swapped during the hold, creates `epoch` in the target on release. With `holders` as the link, `Participant._sweep()` (run on acquire polls and from a holder's `heartbeat()`) unlinks files in the target whose names are 32 lowercase hex digits once the lock object has seen them unchanged for `stale_threshold` (observed with `stale_threshold=2`; the default is 90 s). With `gen` as the link, `GenerationLog._list()` unlinks every 20-digit name except the 64 highest: of 70 such files, it removes the 6 lowest before the acquire fails with `SoftFileLockProtocolError`.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-WXXRI4M4`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The `repro` script drives the files under `repro.d/`.

**`repro`**

import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

SHARED = "/srv/shared"
LOCK_TREE = f"{SHARED}/app.lock.rw"
PROJECT = "/home/victim/project"
HEAD = Path(PROJECT, ".git", "HEAD")
AS_VICTIM = ["runuser", "-u", "victim", "--"]
AS_ATTACKER = ["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--"]
VICTIM_WORKER = [*AS_VICTIM, sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_worker.py"]
ATTACKER_SWAP_TREE = [*AS_ATTACKER, sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/attacker_swap_tree.py"]

# set up: a lock directory anyone may write (0777, no sticky bit), and a git repository only the victim can enter
shutil.rmtree(SHARED, ignore_errors=True)
shutil.rmtree(PROJECT, ignore_errors=True)
os.mkdir(SHARED)
os.chmod(SHARED, 0o777)
subprocess.run([*AS_VICTIM, "git", "init", "--quiet", PROJECT], check=True)
os.chmod(PROJECT, 0o700)
head_before = HEAD.read_text()
print("SETUP    HEAD:", repr(head_before))

attacker_opens_head = subprocess.run(
    [*AS_ATTACKER, sys.executable, "-c", f"open({str(HEAD)!r}, 'w')"], capture_output=True, text=True
)
if attacker_opens_head.returncode == 0:
    sys.exit("setup: the attacker can write HEAD directly")
print("CONTROL  attacker opens HEAD for writing:", attacker_opens_head.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1])

# the victim's long-lived worker does job 1; its lock object creates and checks app.lock.rw
worker = subprocess.Popen(VICTIM_WORKER, stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True)
worker.stdin.write("job 1\n")
worker.stdin.flush()
print("VICTIM  ", worker.stdout.readline().strip())
tree = os.stat(LOCK_TREE)
print("VICTIM   app.lock.rw owner uid", tree.st_uid, "mode", oct(tree.st_mode & 0o777))

# attack: between two jobs, swap in a tree whose gen/ is a symlink to the victim's .git
subprocess.run(ATTACKER_SWAP_TREE, check=True)
print("ATTACK   app.lock.rw/gen ->", os.readlink(f"{LOCK_TREE}/gen"))

# control: a new lock object, in a new victim process, checks the planted tree and refuses it
fresh_worker = subprocess.run(VICTIM_WORKER, input="job 1\n", capture_output=True, text=True)
print("CONTROL  new worker:", (fresh_worker.stdout + fresh_worker.stderr).strip().splitlines()[-1])
print("CONTROL  HEAD after the new worker:", repr(HEAD.read_text()))

# the same worker does job 2 with the lock object that passed the check at job 1
worker.stdin.write("job 2\n")
worker.stdin.close()
print("VICTIM  ", worker.stdout.read().strip())
worker.wait()

# check: HEAD of the victim's private repository must still be git's own
head_after = HEAD.read_text()
print("OBSERVED HEAD:", repr(head_after))
print("OBSERVED .git:", sorted(os.listdir(HEAD.parent)))
git_status = subprocess.run([*AS_VICTIM, "git", "-C", PROJECT, "status"], capture_output=True, text=True)
print("OBSERVED git status:", (git_status.stdout + git_status.stderr).strip().splitlines()[0])
print("BUG" if head_after != head_before and "filelock-rw/1" in head_after else "OK")

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs as root, drops to `victim` and `attacker` through `runuser`, needs `git`, changes no sysctl, and takes about half a second. It creates `/srv/shared` (root-owned, `0777`, no sticky bit), has `victim` run `git init /home/victim/project` and makes that directory `0700`. It then drives two programs. `victim_worker.py` holds one `SoftReadWriteLock("/srv/shared/app.lock")` with default options; for each line on stdin it takes `write_lock(timeout=30)`, releases it and prints `finished <job> and released the lock`. `attacker_swap_tree.py` renames the lock user's `app.lock.rw` aside, creates a new one with a world-writable `holders/`, and makes `app.lock.rw/gen` a symbolic link to `/home/victim/project/.git`, using only write access to `/srv/shared`. On the scanned commit it prints:

```
CONTROL  attacker opens HEAD for writing: PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '/home/victim/project/.git/HEAD'
VICTIM   victim: finished job 1 and released the lock
VICTIM   app.lock.rw owner uid 1000 mode 0o700
ATTACK   app.lock.rw/gen -> /home/victim/project/.git
CONTROL  new worker: RuntimeError: /srv/shared/app.lock.rw/gen exists but is not a directory or is a symlink; refusing to use it
CONTROL  HEAD after the new worker: 'ref: refs/heads/master\n'
VICTIM   victim: finished job 2 and released the lock
OBSERVED HEAD: '<epoch>\nfilelock-rw/1\ngeneration=2\n'
OBSERVED .git: [..., 'epoch', '00000000000000000001', '00000000000000000002', ...]
OBSERVED git status: fatal: not a git repository
BUG
```

The `CONTROL` lines show that the other account cannot reach the repository itself and that a fresh lock object refuses the planted tree. The existing check works; the code does not repeat it for a live instance. The sticky-directory variant ends the same way, with `fs.protected_symlinks=1`. There the other account creates `app.lock.rw`, `gen` and `holders` with mode `0777` in a `1777` parent before the lock user's first acquire, then renames its own `gen` aside and links it to the lock user's `.git`.

Our verification: `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #842 stack head: `OK`, `HEAD` stays `ref: refs/heads/master`, `.git` keeps its original listing and `git status` answers `On branch master`. The result is the same with the stack's owner check disabled, so it does not depend on who owns the tree.

## Impact

With the lock user's privileges, in any directory the lock user can write, the other user gets a file named `HEAD` replaced, new files `epoch`, `HEAD` and 20-digit generation names created (mode `0600`), and files deleted whose names match the protocol's patterns (32 hex digits, 20 digits, `.commit-*`). The bytes written are filelock's own records, not chosen by the other user. Replacing `HEAD` makes a git repository unusable when the other user knows its path. Renaming `<path>.rw` away is something this other user may do anyway, and `docs/how-to.rst` documents the result (a new log starts). What this finding adds is that the lock user's file operations leave the lock's directory.

This is adjacent to GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (`ReadWriteLock` following a symbolic link at its database path, fixed in 4.0.9) and the earlier symbolic link fixes (PR 461 for lock file creation, PR 465 for `SoftFileLock`, PR 565 for refreshing soft read/write lock markers). Each guards the final path component. Here the link sits at a directory component, which `O_NOFOLLOW` does not cover.

## Workarounds

- Keep the lock path in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share a `SoftReadWriteLock` between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory.
- In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, make sure the locking account creates `<path>.rw` before anyone else can (for example at install time with mode `0700`), and do not use a lock path whose `<path>.rw` belongs to another account.
- Prefer a fresh lock object per unit of work over a long-lived singleton when other accounts can write the lock directory. A fresh object re-runs the directory check and refuses a planted tree.

cves.summary:
`StrictSoftFileLock` and `AsyncStrictSoftFileLock` apply the caller's `mode` to the sentinel (the lock file at `<path>`) and to both claim files (the files whose presence says a process wants or holds the lock). They create the two directories that hold the claims, `<path>.filelock` and `<path>.filelock/claims`, with a bare `mkdir()`. That gives `0o777` filtered through the umask (a per-process mask that removes permission bits from new files and directories) or, under a parent with a default ACL (an access control list on a directory that sets the permissions of entries created inside it), through that ACL.

A hold consists of two claim names in that directory, which has no sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it). When the environment leaves another local user (the other user below) a write bit on the directory, that user can unlink the holder's `0600` claims. Three settings do this: umask `000` in a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, umask `002` with the other user in the directory's group, or a default ACL on the lock's parent that grants the group write (the kernel then ignores the umask). After the unlink, the next contender of the holder's account finds the directory empty and enters. The first holder keeps reporting `is_locked == True` and later releases with no error. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.30.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-AD6SUOON`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L, 5.3 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the holder must pass a restrictive `mode` while its umask or the parent's default ACL leaves the other user a write bit on new directories, and a contender of the holder's account must ask for the lock after the claims are gone. With the common umask `022` and no default ACL the directories are `0755`, and the kernel refuses the other user's unlink. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the holder's processes act on their own.

`C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the `0600` claim files stay unreadable. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders then write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:L` (low availability impact): the same write access lets the other user create names in `claims`, and an empty file named `held-v1-<32 zeros>.claim` makes the next `acquire()` raise `SoftFileLockProtocolError` ("malformed claim record") until someone removes it. Classification from the review: security, conditional on a lax umask or a permissive default ACL. The scanner rated it high (CWE-732).

## Scope and preconditions

- The holder passes a restrictive `mode` such as `0o600`. Without one, the umask decides the permissions by documented design (the "File permissions and mode" section of `docs/concepts.rst` defines `mode` only for the lock file). Umask `000` with the default mode gives the same two-holder result but is outside this finding.
- The holder's environment leaves the other user a write bit on new directories. The scanner measured three ways, with `mode=0o600` and the other user a member of group `team`:

  | lock's parent directory | holder's umask | `<path>.filelock` and `claims/` | who can unlink the claims |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `1777`, like `/tmp` | `000` | `0777` | any other local user |
  | `root:team`, `3775` (setgid, so new entries inherit the group, and sticky) | `002` | `2775` | any member of `team` |
  | `root:team`, `1770`, default ACL `group:team:rwx` (`setfacl -d -m g:team:rwx`) | `077` | `0770` | any member of `team` |
  | `root:team`, `3775`, no ACL | `022` | `2755` | no one; the second process times out |

  The default-ACL row is the strongest. A holder with a private umask and `mode=0o600` still gets group-writable claim directories. The lock file in that row is `0600`, because its mode reaches `os.open` and masks the inherited ACL.
- A contender that may enter asks for the lock: another process of the holder's account, or root. Nothing needs planting beforehand. The holder creates and owns the whole tree, so the existing-directory branch of `_ensure_protocol_directory` (the subject of GHSA-9c4x-gm8v-wgc4) plays no part.
- Directories that an affected release already created keep their mode. A `0777` `<path>.filelock` from an earlier run stays writable by other users after an upgrade, because filelock does not remove these directories. Upgraders should `chmod` or remove existing `<path>.filelock` trees (see Workarounds).
- The other lock classes do not have this gap in the same setting. With umask `000` and `mode=0o600`, `FileLock` and `SoftFileLock` create one `0600` file and nothing else, and `SoftReadWriteLock` creates its directories `0700` under any umask. Platform: POSIX permission semantics; demonstrated on Linux.

filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock's user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.

## Mechanism

A process with umask `000` that takes `StrictSoftFileLock("/tmp/<dir>/x.lock", mode=0o600)` leaves this on disk while it holds the lock, every entry owned by the holder:

```
0600 x.lock
0777 x.lock.filelock
0777 x.lock.filelock/claims
0600 x.lock.filelock/claims/held-v1-<token>.claim
0600 x.lock.filelock/claims/intent-v1-<token>.claim
```

Removing a name needs write permission on the directory, and these directories are not sticky. Another local user who cannot read either claim can therefore unlink both. Renaming `claims/` away inside the `0777` `<path>.filelock` has the same effect. For this lock class the directory permissions decide who can end a hold. The sentinel at `<path>` is permanent and says nothing about who holds. A contender starts its doorway by listing the claim directory and proceeds when it is empty. Once the two names are gone, the next contender publishes its own intent and held claims and enters. The original holder does not notice. `is_locked` is its own counter, and `_release` removes its claims by name through `_unlink_owner_path_result`, which takes `FileNotFoundError` as "already removed". The first process therefore releases with exit status 0. No `force_break()`, lifetime or legacy client takes part.

The other user's action is a plain `unlink`. The right to do it comes from filelock's `mkdir`, not from anything the application asked for. In the same setting the other user can neither read nor remove the `0600` sentinel in the sticky parent. With the common umask `022` and no default ACL the directories are `0755`. Other users can then list the claim names, which `mode=0o600` does not suggest either, but cannot remove them, and the second process times out.

## Impact

Another local user who gets a write bit on the claim directories ends a live `StrictSoftFileLock` hold. A second honest process of the holder's account then enters the critical section beside the first. Neither holder receives any signal. This is the overlap the strict lock's fail-closed contract exists to rule out. The same write access lets the other user deny the lock by planting a malformed claim name. This does not disclose the claims' contents (the `0600` claim files stay unreadable), and it does not affect holders whose directories came out `0755` or tighter.

## Workarounds

Run processes that take strict locks with umask `022` or `077`. Do not put a default ACL that grants other accounts write on the lock's parent directory; where you intend group sharing, trust every member of that group with the lock. Keep strict locks in a directory other users cannot write. For paths already in use, `chmod 700` (or remove, while no process holds the lock) every existing `<path>.filelock` tree. Its mode comes from creation time and nothing changes it afterwards: `find <dir> -maxdepth 1 -type d -name '*.filelock' -exec chmod -R go-w {} +`.

## Mechanism

The owner of a directory can unlink and rename every entry in it, whatever the entries' own owner and mode. A strict hold consists of two names, `intent-v1-<token>.claim` and `held-v1-<token>.claim`, in `<path>.filelock/claims`. The sentinel (the lock file at `<path>`) is permanent and says nothing about who holds. When the other user runs the equivalent of `mkdir -m 777 -p work.lock.filelock/claims` before the lock user first uses `work.lock`, every lock user acquire publishes its claims into a directory the other user can empty. Lock user process A acquires and holds. The other user unlinks both of A's claims; both `unlink` calls succeed, because write permission on the directory is enough.

Lock user process B calls `acquire()` while A is inside its critical section. `_attempt_doorway` starts with `if _read_existing_claims(...): return False`, which turns a contender away while a holder exists, but the scan is now empty. B publishes its own intent and held claims, sees only those in the later rescans, and wins.

A is not told. A strict holder does not look at its claims between acquire and release, and on release `_unlink_owner_path_result` takes the `FileNotFoundError` for each missing claim as "already removed", so `_release` finishes without error. The break involves neither a `lifetime` nor a lease, and neither `break_lock()` nor `force_break()`. The benign path shows what the check is missing. When the lock user's first acquire creates the directories itself they are `0755` and owned by the lock user (umask `022`). The other user's `unlink` then fails with `EACCES`, its `rename` or `rmdir` of `work.lock.filelock` fails with `EPERM` under the sticky bit, and B raises `Timeout`.

`OsFiles.prepare` has the same gap for `SoftReadWriteLock`. The code suppresses `EEXIST` from `mkdir(mode=0o700)`, and the check that follows looks only at `S_ISDIR` and `S_ISLNK`. The class docstring's protection against "same-host different-UID users via `0o600` / `0o700` permissions" therefore holds only for whoever gets there first. With the other user owning `/tmp/app.lock.rw`, `gen` and `holders` before the lock user first uses `SoftReadWriteLock("/tmp/app.lock")`, the scanner observed the following, with the same two accounts.

**Creates and renames redirected through a symlink.** The other user's tree holds a generation log (the record of who holds the lock, under `gen/`) naming a live writer, so the lock user polls. Once the lock user's record appears in `holders/` (its `prepare()` is over), the other user renames `gen` aside and puts a symlink to `/home/victim/project/.git`, a repository inside a `0700` directory, in its place. The lock user's `write_lock()` returns without error. By then `GenerationLog.commit()` has created `epoch`, `00000000000000000001` and `00000000000000000002` in `.git` and renamed a record over `.git/HEAD`, which now reads `<epoch>\nfilelock-rw/1\ngeneration=2\n`, owned by the lock user; `git status` answers `fatal: not a git repository`. With `holders` swapped instead, `Participant._sweep()` unlinks files with 32-hex-digit names in the target directory once they have stayed unchanged for `stale_threshold`. This needs no race: every later acquisition on an instance that has passed `prepare()` goes through the swapped `gen`.

**Two writers, no `on_compromise`.** `OsFiles.read()` accepts any regular file, so the owner of `gen` writes snapshots itself. While lock user process V1 is inside `write_lock()`, the other user creates the next `gen/<N>` naming no holder, and V2's `write_lock(timeout=2)` succeeds at once. A further forged generation naming both tokens keeps both heartbeats answering `ok`, because `Participant.heartbeat()` tests only `self.token in latest.members`; `compromise` was still `None` in both after the default 30 s heartbeat. The other user reads no lock user record at any point: listing `gen/` and `holders/` gives the generation and the tokens.

**Hangs, memory growth and bare `OSError`s.** The protocol code treats every record in `gen/` and `holders/` as written by a cooperating peer, so the tree's owner can do several things. They can make `Participant.leave()` retry a refused commit without end (`read_lock(timeout=1)` spins at full CPU instead of raising `Timeout`). They can keep `GenerationLog._probe()` walking by appending records ahead of it (3 s of writes kept `read_lock(timeout=1)` busy for about 60 s). They can make every `acquire_write(timeout=1)` and `release()` on a free lock take about 22 s with 200 000 generation names hard-linked into a sticky `gen/` (a hard link is a second name for the same file), which `_list()` and `_compact_through()` walk again on each poll because `OsFiles.unlink()` swallows the `EPERM`.

They can also pin 1 MiB of the lock user's memory per sparse file planted in `holders/`, because `Ledger.observe()` keeps every swept record whole (2 000 hard links to one 1 MiB file: 2 028 MiB resident when `acquire_write()` returns). Under an address-space limit the sweep raises `MemoryError` inside the heartbeat thread, which nothing handles, so the record is not refreshed again. After `stale_threshold` a second lock user process gets the write lock while the first still has `compromise` `None`. And they can make every acquire of a free lock raise a bare `OSError` with a mode-`000` orphan in `holders/` or a symlink at `gen/HEAD`. None of these is reachable in a tree the lock user created itself: it is `0700` at all three levels and the other user's writes fail with `EACCES`.

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer (`victim` uid 1000, `attacker` uid 1001, lock `work.lock` in a root-owned `1777` directory under `/tmp`, `StrictSoftFileLock(path, timeout=1)`, Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14.8, overlayfs) runs the same contention twice. In the control round on `control.lock`, whose directories `victim` creates, it prints `claims is owned by victim`, the unlinks by `attacker` answer `Permission denied`, the first process prints `['acquired', 'is_locked=True', 'released']` and the second `['Timeout']`. In the observed round on `work.lock`, planted by `attacker`, it prints `claims is owned by attacker` and `removed held-v1-….claim; removed intent-v1-….claim`, and both processes print `['acquired', 'is_locked=True', 'released']`, the second having acquired before the first was let out. The verdict line reads `control_excludes=True both_inside=True` and then `BUG` after about 2 s. The scanner ran the variant that plants only the outer `<path>.filelock` (then renames the `claims` of `victim` aside) by hand with the same result, and each `SoftReadWriteLock` effect listed under Mechanism in its own run with the same two accounts.

Our review ran the reproducer against the 4.2.0 release image and the scanned commit (`BUG` on both) and against the head of #839 (`OK`). The review's regression tests for both sites need a sticky `/tmp` of another UID and ran there.

## Impact

Another local user who can create names in the lock's directory puts two processes of the lock user, root included, into the same `StrictSoftFileLock` critical section at a moment of the other user's choosing, with no exception or other signal to either. Two processes then modify whatever the lock protects at the same time.

Against `SoftReadWriteLock` the same position decides when two writers, or a writer and readers, are inside together and keeps `compromise` silent in all of them. It also gets file operations made with the lock user's privileges (root's, for a root service) in any directory the lock user can write: a file named `HEAD` replaced, files named `epoch` and `0000000000000000000N` created, files with 32-hex-digit names deleted. The bytes written are filelock's own records, not content the other user chooses. It can keep the lock user's acquire or release running past any `timeout`, or grow the lock user's memory by 1 MiB per planted file. It is **not** a disclosure of the lock user's data, and it does not reach a path the lock user has already used while that tree still exists.

## Workarounds

Keep strict and soft read-write locks in a directory other users cannot write, rather than `/tmp` or another sticky shared directory. Where a shared directory is unavoidable, create `<path>.filelock/claims` (or `<path>.rw` with `gen` and `holders`) as the service user before any other account can, for example at install or boot, and check `stat -c %U` of an existing tree before the first use. A tmp cleaner, a reboot or the `<path>.rw` recovery removes the tree and reopens the window. The kernel refuses a planted `0755` strict tree (the lock user's acquire fails with `PermissionError`), so an acquire that raises that error on a new path without a known cause is worth investigating.

cves.summary:
filelock on Windows ignores the `mode` argument. `FileLock(path, mode=0o600)` creates the same file as `FileLock(path)`: one with no security descriptor of its own (the Windows record that says who may access a file). Its access list, or ACL, is whatever the lock directory hands down to new files. filelock creates the `ReadWriteLock` database, which it asks to be `0o600`, the same way. In a directory whose inheritable ACL grants other local accounts access to new files, those accounts can open the lock file or database. They can take the byte-range lock (a lock on a span of bytes in a file) once the owner releases it and keep the owner's later `acquire()` calls waiting or timing out. They can read holder metadata an `on_acquired` hook left in a `preserve_lock_file=True` file. Where the directory hands down modify access, they can write to both files.

`lock.mode` still reports `0o600`. The documentation neither promises an ACL on Windows nor says that Windows drops the mode. On Unix the same mode keeps other accounts out. Mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol holds on either platform. Affected versions are filelock 3.10.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. Finding covered by this advisory:

- `ANT-2026-0KEO0DDO` [medium, CWE-732]: WindowsFileLock ignores mode; 0o600 lock files inherit the directory ACL.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L` scores 5.3 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other account needs a logon on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): no race. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the lock file (holder metadata) and the lock database are readable where `0o600` was meant to keep them private. `I:L` (partial integrity impact): in the directory layout the maintainers tested, the other account can also write both files, which lets it corrupt the lock's own state but nothing the lock protects. `A:L` (partial availability impact): the other account can hold the byte-range lock and make the owner wait or time out. `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the review: **Windows permission failure with security impact only where callers rely on `mode=0o600` across accounts**. The review had marked it an unconfirmed Windows claim, since the scanner traced stand-in Win32 calls on Linux. The maintainers have since confirmed it on Windows with two local accounts (see Evidence). The scanner rated this medium; the maintainers keep medium.

## Scope and preconditions

- The affected classes are `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Windows (`WindowsFileLock`), and the SQLite database of `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`. Both go through `_open_non_reparse_fd`. The soft locks create their markers with `os.open`, which also keeps only a read-only bit of the mode on Windows; the scanner did not examine them further.
- The directory is one that other local accounts cannot write, which the documentation already requires on Windows, but whose inheritable entries grant them read (or modify) access to new files. Examples are a service's data directory readable by `Users`, or any directory with `(OI)(CI)` entries (entries that new files and sub-directories inherit) for another account. A directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts, such as one inside a user profile, hides the problem.
- The other account must open the file. According to the `LockFileEx` documentation, read access is enough to take the byte-range lock, so it can hold the lock whenever the owner does not. The lock file exists while the owner holds the lock, and stays after release with `preserve_lock_file=True`. The `ReadWriteLock` database is not unlinked at any point.
- Unix is not affected, because `UnixFileLock` creates the file with the mode and repeats it with `fchmod`. Mutual exclusion between cooperating processes is not affected.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_open_non_reparse_fd` reduces the mode to one `read_only` bit](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L252-L253). That bit is false for every accepted mode, because [`_check_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L526) rejects any mode without owner read and write, and an unset mode becomes `0o666`. In [`_nt_open`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L283-L310) the `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES.SecurityDescriptor` field stays unassigned, and `read_only` only chooses `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY`. [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1086) passes `0o600` through the same function on Windows.

## Introduced

[d0061e4](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d0061e4643df) "added multiuser support and associated tests" ([#192](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/192), 2023-03-15), first tag 3.10.0 (verified), added the `mode` parameter and on Windows handed it to `os.open`, which applies only the read-only attribute. The Windows backend has applied no more of the mode than that at any version, so this is a long-standing gap rather than a regression.

## Mechanism

`_open_non_reparse_fd(path, mode)` computes `read_only = not mode & _OWNER_WRITE` and calls `_nt_open(path, read_only=read_only)`. `_nt_open` fills an `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` with the NT path and `OBJ_CASE_INSENSITIVE` and leaves `SecurityDescriptor` NULL. It then calls `NtCreateFile` with `FILE_OPEN_IF` and `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL` (or `FILE_ATTRIBUTE_READONLY` when `read_only`, which no accepted mode produces). Nothing consults the group and other bits. Per the `NtCreateFile` and `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` documentation, a NULL descriptor gives the new file default security, which on NTFS is the set of inheritable entries of the parent directory. A lock file created with `mode=0o600` in a directory that hands down read access to `Users` is therefore readable by `Users`.

Nothing tells the caller. The constructor validates the mode, `lock.mode` returns `0o600`, and `has_explicit_mode` is `True`. `docs/concepts.rst` says "filelock creates the file with it" and that "`0o600` and `0o700` keep other UIDs out", with no Windows caveat. Only the `_open_non_reparse_fd` docstring and a comment in `_soft.py` record the limitation.

cves.summary:
`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) run `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` on a fresh connection for every acquire. That statement makes SQLite load the whole schema (the `sqlite_master` table, which lists every table and index with its `CREATE` text) of whatever file sits at the lock path. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout`, which bounds waits for another connection's lock, not schema loading. The only content checks reject non-regular files and WAL mode (write-ahead log, an SQLite mode that keeps changes in a side file). A local user who can place or overwrite the file at a `ReadWriteLock`'s database path can therefore make every `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` of every process using that lock ignore its `timeout` and `blocking=False`. That position needs a non-sticky shared directory, or a database owned by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) that other users may write.

One 37 KB crafted file stalls each acquire for as long as its author chooses while the process allocates about 1 GB. A second 28 KB layout makes the acquire of a free lock run without end, spinning at 100% CPU and ignoring Ctrl-C. The effect is availability only: the other user reads nothing and corrupts nothing. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-NFPRHMYJ` [medium, CWE-400]: ReadWriteLock: crafted lock database hangs acquire regardless of timeout.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` scores 5.5 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the other user plants one file; no race. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `A:H` (high availability impact): every acquire of every process using the lock runs for as long as that user chose, or does not return, with `timeout` and `blocking=False` ignored and `SIGINT` not delivered, so only killing the process ends it. `C:N` and `I:N` (no confidentiality or integrity impact): the other user reads nothing and corrupts nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, an availability concern only when an untrusted actor can supply the database file (it needs a writable or replaceable database path). The scanner rated it medium. The review agrees with the mechanism and the precondition.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other party is a different local account that can create or replace the file at the lock path. One way: the lock directory is writable by that account and not sticky (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it), for example a group-writable project or cache directory. There the account can be the first to create the database, or rename the lock user's database aside and put the crafted one in its place. The other way: the lock user's own database is writable by that account (`0666`), which is the setup a lock shared between accounts needs. In a `1777` directory the scanner wrote the crafted file over such a database in place, and the lock user's next acquire hung. The lock user must be able to open the file read-write, so a file the other user creates is `0666`.
- Sticky directories and kernel settings. In a sticky world-writable directory such as `/tmp`, Linux with `fs.protected_regular=2` (a kernel setting) refuses the lock user's `O_CREAT` open of a file owned by the other account with `EACCES`. A database owned by the other user does not work there. That does not cover a `0666` database owned by the lock user. The scanner did not test systems with `fs.protected_regular=0` (the kernel's own default).
- Platform. Every platform runs the same statements. On Windows the documentation already requires a lock directory that untrusted users cannot write, so the shared-directory setup is outside what the project supports there.
- Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_configure_and_begin` runs `PRAGMA busy_timeout=...; PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY;` on a fresh connection](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L814-L816), and for a read lock [`SELECT name FROM sqlite_master LIMIT 1` at line 832](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L832). The code in [`_do_acquire_inner` closes the previous connection and opens a new one on every acquire](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L745-L754). The only content checks are [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) (regular file) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) (20 header bytes).

## Introduced

The acquire path dates from `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)", 2026-02-12), first released in **3.20.4** (verified: `git tag --contains cfd4446` gives 3.20.4). Since #657 (3.30.0) the lock reopens the connection on every acquire, so the stall repeats on every acquire rather than once per instance.

## Mechanism

`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` is the first statement that needs the schema. SQLite reads every row of `sqlite_master` and parses each row's `sql` text there. Run one at a time on the crafted file, `PRAGMA busy_timeout` returns at once and `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` takes the whole time. The read-mode `SELECT` needs the schema too. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout` (lines 814 to 816 and 823 to 826), which limits how long SQLite waits for another connection's file lock. Loading the schema is not a wait, so nothing limits it. `blocking=False` and `timeout=0` reach SQLite as `busy_timeout=0` and stall the same way (2.4 s each with a 5-row file). `acquire_write` runs the same pragma. `AsyncReadWriteLock.read_lock(timeout=1)` stalls the same way (4.7 s with 10 rows; wrapping the acquire in `asyncio.wait_for(..., 2)` does not return earlier). A second `acquire_read` on the same instance stalls for as long as the first.

The constructor is not affected. Its validation connection (lines 484 and 485) runs no statement, so the lock user sees nothing until the first acquire. A stack dump taken 2 s into the stall shows the thread in `_configure_and_begin` at the `executescript` call. The lock accepts any SQLite file that is a regular file and not in WAL mode, whoever created it. Two layouts reach the load, at the same statement and with the same preconditions.

**Long schema rows.** Each `sqlite_master` row is `('table', 't0001', 't0001', 2, 'CREATE TABLE t0001(x) --AAAA…')` with an `sql` text of 999,999,024 bytes, under SQLite's 1,000,000,000-byte limit. The file does not store the text. Each row's cell names page 2 as its first overflow page (a page that holds the part of a row too large for its own page), and the "next overflow page" field of page 2 names page 2 again. SQLite builds each row from the same 4 KB page, read about 244,000 times over. The header claims 244,142 pages, because SQLite rejects a record larger than page size times page count. The script extends the file to that length as a hole (unallocated space that reads as zeros), because SQLite also rejects a file shorter than its header claims. Eight rows fit in one 4 KB leaf page. The statements are valid `CREATE TABLE`s, so SQLite reports no error, and after the stall the acquire succeeds; it does not raise `Timeout`.

Measured with `read_lock(timeout=1)`: 1 row, 12,288 bytes on disk, returns after 0.6 s; 10 rows, 16,384 bytes, 4.8 s; 50 rows, 36,864 bytes, 23 s. Peak RSS (resident set size, the memory the process holds) is 981 MB in every case, because memory stays at one row's worth; the cost is about 0.47 s per row. Under a 512 MiB address-space limit the same acquire raises `MemoryError` from line 816.

**Looping interior pages.** The long rows are one way in, not the cause: SQLite loads whatever schema the file holds, with no bound. A 20 KB file with no long rows, whose three index pages each point 200 times at the same child page (8,000,000 leaves), stalls `read_lock(timeout=1)` for 8 s with 10 MB of memory. Each extra level multiplies the time by the fan-out (the number of children per page).

At the largest fan-out SQLite accepts, the stall becomes a hang. In a 28,672-byte file of seven 4 KB pages, pages 1 to 6 are `sqlite_master` interior pages whose 660 cell pointers all name one 5-byte cell. That cell's child and the page's right-most child are both the next page, and page 7 is a leaf with one row of five NULLs. SQLite 3.40.1 refuses a page with more than 681 cells and a tree deeper than 20 pages, but does not notice that it reaches a page more than once. Each level therefore multiplies the rows of `sqlite_master` by 661.

The row is not a valid schema entry, and that does not stop the scan: SQLite raises `sqlite3.DatabaseError: malformed database schema (?)` only after the last row. One level raises `DatabaseError` at once. Two levels (12 KiB) give 436,921 rows after 0.16 s. Six levels (28 KiB) give 661⁶, about 8 × 10¹⁶ rows, still at line 816 with 30 s of CPU time used when killed after 30 s. On that file `acquire_write(timeout=1)`, `acquire_read(blocking=False)` and `acquire_read(timeout=0)` spin on the same line. `SIGINT` does not raise `KeyboardInterrupt` (the process was still running at 100% CPU 4 s after `kill -INT`), because the thread does not leave the one SQLite call.

**`repro.d/make_stalling_db.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# usage: make_stalling_db.py <database path> <number of schema rows>
#
# Writes a SQLite database whose sqlite_master rows each carry ~1 GB of `sql` text, stored in a few 4 KB pages:
# every row's text continues on one overflow page whose "next overflow page" field names itself.
import os
import struct
import sys

database, schema_rows = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])

PAGE_SIZE = 4096
LOOP_PAGE = 2
COMMENT_LEN = 999_999_000  # keeps each sql text just under SQLite's 1,000,000,000-byte string limit
CLAIMED_PAGES = COMMENT_LEN // PAGE_SIZE + 2  # SQLite refuses a record longer than page size x pages in the file
TABLE_INTERIOR_PAGE, TABLE_LEAF_PAGE = 0x05, 0x0D

def varint(value):
    groups = [value & 0x7F]
    while value := value >> 7:
        groups.insert(0, value & 0x7F | 0x80)
    return bytes(groups)

def schema_row_cell(rowid):
    # the row ('table', name, name, 2, 'CREATE TABLE name(x) --AAAA...'): a valid statement, so SQLite reports no error
    name = b"t%04d" % rowid
    sql_start = b"CREATE TABLE " + name + b"(x) --"
    sql_len = len(sql_start) + COMMENT_LEN
    serial_types = b"".join(varint(t) for t in [13 + 2 * 5, 13 + 2 * len(name), 13 + 2 * len(name), 1, 13 + 2 * sql_len])
    record_start = varint(1 + len(serial_types)) + serial_types + b"table" + name + name + b"\x02" + sql_start
    record_len = len(record_start) + COMMENT_LEN
    # the file format's rule for how much of an overflowing table-leaf record stays on the leaf page
    min_local, max_local = (PAGE_SIZE - 12) * 32 // 255 - 23, PAGE_SIZE - 35
    local = min_local + (record_len - min_local) % (PAGE_SIZE - 4)
    if local > max_local:
        local = min_local
    return varint(record_len) + varint(rowid) + record_start.ljust(local, b"A") + struct.pack(">I", LOOP_PAGE)

def btree_page(page_type, cells, right_child=b"", header_offset=0):
    page = bytearray(PAGE_SIZE)
    content_start = PAGE_SIZE
    cell_pointers = b""
    for cell in cells:
        content_start -= len(cell)
        page[content_start : content_start + len(cell)] = cell
        cell_pointers += struct.pack(">H", content_start)
    header = struct.pack(">BHHHB", page_type, 0, len(cells), content_start, 0) + right_child + cell_pointers
    page[header_offset : header_offset + len(header)] = header
    return page

# pages 3 and up: the leaves of sqlite_master, about eight rows each
cells = [schema_row_cell(rowid) for rowid in range(1, schema_rows + 1)]
rows_per_leaf = (PAGE_SIZE - 8) // (len(cells[0]) + 2)
leaves = [btree_page(TABLE_LEAF_PAGE, cells[i : i + rows_per_leaf]) for i in range(0, schema_rows, rows_per_leaf)]

# page 2: the overflow page, pointing at itself, then 4092 bytes of comment text
loop_page = struct.pack(">I", LOOP_PAGE) + b"A" * (PAGE_SIZE - 4)

# page 1: the database header, then the root of sqlite_master with one child per leaf
first_leaf, last_leaf = 3, 3 + len(leaves) - 1
children = [struct.pack(">I", first_leaf + i) + varint((i + 1) * rows_per_leaf) for i in range(len(leaves) - 1)]
root_page = btree_page(TABLE_INTERIOR_PAGE, children, right_child=struct.pack(">I", last_leaf), header_offset=100)
root_page[:100] = b"".join([
    b"SQLite format 3\0",
    struct.pack(">H", PAGE_SIZE),
    bytes([1, 1]),  # file format versions: rollback journal, not WAL (which ReadWriteLock refuses)
    bytes([0, 64, 32, 32]),  # reserved bytes per page and the three fixed payload fractions
    struct.pack(">I", 1),  # file change counter
    struct.pack(">I", CLAIMED_PAGES),  # database size in pages
    struct.pack(">II", 0, 0),  # no freelist
    struct.pack(">II", 1, 4),  # schema cookie, schema format
    struct.pack(">II", 0, 0),  # default cache size, no auto-vacuum
    struct.pack(">I", 1),  # text encoding: UTF-8
    struct.pack(">III", 0, 0, 0),  # user version, incremental vacuum, application id
    bytes(20),
    struct.pack(">I", 1),  # version-valid-for equals the change counter, so SQLite trusts the page count above
    struct.pack(">I", 3040001),  # SQLite version that wrote the file
])

with open(database, "wb") as file:
    file.write(root_page + loop_page + b"".join(leaves))
    written = file.tell()
    file.truncate(CLAIMED_PAGES * PAGE_SIZE)  # SQLite also refuses a file shorter than it claims; this stays a hole
os.chmod(database, 0o666)  # the victim's ReadWriteLock opens the database read-write
print(f"attacker: wrote {database}: {schema_rows} schema rows in {written} bytes, apparent size {CLAIMED_PAGES * PAGE_SIZE}")
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs as root and drops to `attacker` and `victim`. It recreates `/tmp/shared-cache` with mode `0777` and no sticky bit. It runs `make_stalling_db.py /tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db 50` as `attacker`. That script writes the header and the `sqlite_master` root on page 1, the self-referencing overflow page on page 2, and leaf pages holding 50 valid `CREATE TABLE tNNNN(x) --AAAA…` rows whose text runs to under 1 GB through page 2, extended to the claimed page count as a hole, mode `0666`. It then runs `victim_reader.py` (`ReadWriteLock(path)` and one `with lock.read_lock(timeout=1):`) as `victim` and times it:

```
attacker: wrote /tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db: 50 schema rows in 36864 bytes, apparent size 1000005632
lock database uses 36864 bytes of disk
victim: read_lock(timeout=1) acquired after 24.6 s
victim process ran for 24.8 s, peak RSS 981 MB
BUG
```

The verdict is `BUG` when the `victim` process, whose only work is an acquire with a one-second timeout, ran for more than 10 s. A separate script in the report (`looping_db.py`) builds the looping file; the same `victim_reader.py` run on it as `victim` does not return. A `victim` process that had already used the lock stalled on its next acquire after the other user swapped the file under it. In a `1777` directory a `0666` database owned by `victim`, overwritten in place with the looping file, hung the next acquire.

Our verification: `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 image (`e2e7d70`). On the PR #834 head the `victim` process stops with a `ValueError` after 0.1 s at 24 MB peak RSS and the reproducer prints `OK`.

## Impact

Another local user who can create or replace the lock database makes every `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` of every process using that `ReadWriteLock` run for a time of their choosing (about 500 bytes of disk per extra half second) while allocating about 1 GB, or not return at all, regardless of `timeout` or `blocking=False`. This goes beyond what holding the lock gives that user, because a held lock ends in `Timeout` when the caller's timeout runs out, and this does not. With the looping-page layout the acquiring thread spins at 100% of one CPU on a free lock, `Timeout` is not raised, Ctrl-C does not interrupt it, and only killing the process ends it. It is a denial of service of the lock user's process only: it reads nothing and corrupts nothing, and in the long-row case the lock is still granted afterwards.

## Workarounds

- Keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.
- Do not give the lock a database another account may write. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. A lock shared between accounts through a `0666` database stays reachable even in `/tmp`.
- If a stall or hang appears, the file at the lock path is the cause; replacing it with an empty file restores the lock.

cwe.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption

cves.summary:
`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS` decide from the record inside the marker file whether its owner is gone. The marker is the file whose presence says a process holds the lock. They do not check who could have written that record.

A local user who can write the marker but cannot remove it rewrites the holder's record to name a dead PID (process id). That position arises with an explicit `mode` with group or other write bits, or the default mode under a lax umask (the process setting that strips permission bits from new files), in a sticky or otherwise non-removable directory. The sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it. The next contender running as the holder's account, or root, judges the lock stale, removes the live marker on that user's behalf and acquires it. Two processes then run the critical section together and neither gets an error. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-W1H9NXUH`).

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N` scores 4.7 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the marker must carry group or other write bits (an explicit permissive `mode`, or umask `002`/`000` with a shared group), and a contender of the holder's account must ask for the lock while the forged record is in place. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders then write whatever the lock protects, and the holder is not told. `C:N` and `A:N` (no confidentiality or availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged). Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on another user being able to write the live marker. The scanner rated it high (CWE-345). The default mode under umask `022` is not affected.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can write the marker. The application passes a `mode` with group or other write bits, which `fchmod` applies as given since 4.1.0. `0o666` is a common choice for a lock shared between accounts, although a soft-lock contender of another account waits as well on a `0o644` marker, since contenders only read and rename. Or the application uses the default mode (`0o666` through the umask) under umask `002` in a directory whose group the other user belongs to, or under umask `000`. The default mode under umask `022` is not affected.
- The other user cannot remove the marker itself: the directory is sticky, or the other user cannot write it at all (a `0755` directory owned by the lock's user gives the same overlap). In a non-sticky shared directory the other user can unlink the marker without filelock, and filelock adds nothing.
- A contender that may rename the marker asks for the lock: another process of the holder's account (several workers of one user) or root. A contender of another unprivileged account cannot rename the marker in a sticky directory and times out.
- The finding reaches every class that publishes a soft marker: `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async variants, and `FileLock(mode=0o666)` on a filesystem where `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file) fails with `ENOSYS`.

These protections against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496: the create mode in [`SoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L67-L71), the explicit-mode `fchmod` in [`_apply_explicit_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L100-L105), the trusting verdict in [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) and the [`owner_is_stale`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_identity.py#L64-L79) it relies on; the same call in [`MarkerSoftFileLock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_marker.py#L74-L81) and [`SoftFileLease`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_lease.py#L229-L256).

## Introduced

The stale verdict that trusts the record came in with e35c3afac473 ("feat(soft): detect and break stale locks", #476, 2026-02-13), first released in 3.22.0. From then on a marker left group- or other-writable by the umask is forgeable. The reproducer's exact configuration, an explicit `mode=0o666` under umask `022`, needs 66d309d ("fix(soft): honour mode and tighten marker grammar", #807), first released in 4.1.0. Both match the git tags.

## Mechanism

A contender whose `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` create fails with `EEXIST` goes to `_try_break_stale_lock`. `_read_lock_file` makes sure the path is a regular file (`lstat`, `O_NOFOLLOW` open, `fstat`) and returns its content, mtime and inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). It has the `fstat` result in hand but does not look at `st_uid` or `st_mode`. The code parses the content into `pid`, `hostname` and start token and hands them to `owner_is_stale`, whose docstring promises to return `True` "only when this process can prove the exact recorded owner is dead". That proof holds only if the owner wrote the record. A process of another account that can open the marker for writing uses `O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC` (no `O_CREAT`, so `fs.protected_regular` does not block it) and writes `2147483647\n<host>\n`, keeping the host line. The host matches, PID 2147483647 does not exist, and `owner_is_stale` returns `True`.

`break_lock_file` renames the marker to `<lock>.break.<pid>.<token>` and unlinks it. Its mtime and inode guard compares against what the contender read after the rewrite, so it passes. The contender, which runs as the marker's owner, does the rename, so the sticky bit allows it. On the next poll the contender's `O_EXCL` create succeeds. The first holder is not told: `SoftFileLock` has no heartbeat, and on release `_unlink_open_marker` finds another inode or no file at the path and returns without an error.

Other records lead to the same break, each run by the scanner the same way: the holder's own PID and host with a different third line (`owner_is_stale` reads a live PID with another start token as a recycled PID); an empty file (malformed, broken after `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD`, 2 s). `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` apply `owner_is_stale` to the `pid=`, `host=` and `start=` fields of a protocol 2 record, and rewriting `pid=` admitted a second process for both. A `SoftFileLease` holder learns of it at its next heartbeat through `on_compromise`; `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` holders do not learn of it at all.

The marker becomes writable by another account in two ways. An explicit `mode` with group or other write bits goes through `fchmod`, so the umask does not narrow it (`test_lock_mode_soft` at the scanned commit pins `-rw-rw-rw-` under umask `022`). The default mode passes `0o666` to `os.open`, so under umask `002` the marker is `0o664`. With no `mode` argument, in a setgid and sticky group directory (`3770`), a second member of the group rewrote the marker and a second process of the holder's user acquired the same way. ## Impact

A local user who can write a soft lock's marker but cannot remove it gets a second process admitted into the critical section while the first holder is still inside. With no `lifetime` set, `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` give neither process a signal. Whatever the lock protects (a cache, an install directory, a state file) then has two concurrent writers. The other user chooses the moment and gains nothing else: it touches no file other than the marker. The process that rewrites the record runs under a different UID from the holder; the same-UID contender only follows the protocol.

## Workarounds

Do not give soft markers group or other write bits: pass no `mode` (or `mode=0o644`) under umask `022`. The write bits matter only for the native `flock` lock and for `FileLock`'s first open before it falls back to a soft lock. Avoid umask `002` or `000` for processes that take soft locks in directories shared with other accounts, and keep lock files in a directory other users cannot write.

## Scope and preconditions

- The affected classes are `SoftFileLock` and everything that reuses its `_acquire`: `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, the async soft locks, and `FileLock` after an `ENOSYS` fallback to a soft lock. `UnixFileLock` itself does not call the helper. `WindowsFileLock._acquire()` does, but on Windows `os.access` reads the link's own read-only attribute and does not follow it; that branch did not run.
- The other user must be able to create entries in the lock's directory. With Linux defaults (`fs.protected_symlinks=1`) the kernel refuses the lock user's attempt to follow another user's symlink in a directory that is both sticky and world-writable. `/tmp` therefore gives `PermissionError` for every target and leaks nothing. A `0777` directory without the sticky bit, or a sticky group-writable one (`1770` with a shared group), has no such cover and leaks as described. macOS and the BSDs have no `fs.protected_symlinks`, and a symlink there has mode bits of its own, so one without the owner-write bit would reach `os.access` with no swap at all (not executed).
- The swap is practical only with a second CPU for the other user.
- The other user needs to see how the lock user's acquire ended, for example the exception in a shared log, an exit status, or when the job stopped (`PermissionError` ends a blocking acquire within about a second; the other case runs to its timeout). The scanner also observed a variant that needs no output from the lock user. Hold the soft lock, set the marker (the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock) to mode `0o066`, swap the symlink in and out for a few seconds, release, and see whether a marker owned by the other uid appears. A contender still waiting takes the lock; one that raised is gone.

## Introduced

[#567](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/567) (022394c, first tag 3.29.5) had changed the helper from `os.stat` to `os.lstat` so that a symlink planted at the lock path could not probe its target.

## Mechanism

`SoftFileLock._acquire` calls the helper first, once per `poll_interval` (0.05 s by default) for as long as the lock user waits. The helper runs `os.lstat(path)`. When the node has no `S_IWUSR` it runs `os.access(path, os.W_OK, effective_ids=...)` without `follow_symlinks=False`. On current Linux that is `faccessat2(AT_FDCWD, path, W_OK, AT_EACCESS)`, which resolves a symlink. If that returns false, a second `os.lstat` confirms a node is still there and the helper raises `PermissionError`. The other user's planted file has mode `0466`: no owner-write bit, which sends the helper on to `os.access`, and other-writable, so that `os.access` on the file itself says yes. The other user alternates the file and a symlink at the path (`os.replace` of a fresh symlink, then `os.replace` of a hard link to the marker; the lock would evict a symlink left for 2 s as a malformed marker).

One call of the helper then goes one of three ways. First, `lstat` sees the symlink (mode `0777` on Linux, `S_IWUSR` set), `os.access` is not called, the helper returns. Second, `lstat` sees the file and `os.access` sees the file: true, returns. Third, `lstat` sees the file and `os.access` sees the symlink, resolved to its target with the lock user's permissions: returns if the lock user may write the target, otherwise raises `PermissionError`. After a return, the `O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW` open fails with `EEXIST` and the poll ends as "lock is held". `PermissionError` therefore comes only from the third way and only for a target the lock user cannot write, and it leaves `acquire()` at once instead of after the timeout.

The scanner measured what the outcome encodes with 4 000 non-blocking acquires per target as `victim` (uid 1000, `0700` private directory). An existing file or directory of `victim`: 0 `PermissionError`. A missing name there gives 311 to 339. A `0444` file of `victim`: 433 to 460. `/etc/passwd` or `/etc/shadow`: 237 to 422. With root taking the lock the answer is plain existence, 0 for `/etc/shadow` and `/root/.bashrc`, 366 for a missing name under `/root`. A symlink alone at the path, without the swap, tells nothing (2 000 `Timeout` of 2 000 for both targets, then evicted as malformed after 2 s).

The hard-link route into a sticky directory such as `/tmp` needs `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`, a Linux kernel setting.
